title: Animals without backbones: worms, snails, crabs, spiders, insects, starfish and jellyfish

summary.text: This unit is about animals that have no backbone. Your backbone is the long chain of small bones down the middle of your back. Fish, frogs, lizards, birds and mammals have one. But worms, snails, crabs, spiders, insects, starfish and jellyfish do not. They hold their bodies up in other ways. A worm uses water held tight inside it. A snail carries a shell. Crabs, spiders and insects wear hard armour on the outside. A jellyfish lets the sea hold it up. About 95 out of every 100 kinds of animal that people have named have no backbone. So animals like us are the unusual ones.
summary.art: A child lying on the grass with a magnifying glass, and around her, drawn in a circle, an earthworm, a snail, a crab, a spider, an ant, a starfish and a jellyfish, with one small sparrow at the edge.

intro.hook: Bend forward and ask someone to run a finger gently down the middle of your back. Can you feel the row of bumps? Now think of an earthworm. Where are its bumps?
intro.text: The bumps you felt are your backbone. It is a chain of small bones that holds you up. A worm has no backbone at all. Neither does a snail, a spider or an ant. Yet a worm can push through hard soil, and an ant can carry a crumb heavier than itself. So how do they hold their bodies up? And here is a surprise. If you counted every kind of animal on Earth, the ones without a backbone would win by miles. This unit is about them.
intro.art: A child bent forward while a parent's finger traces the bumps of the backbone, and beside them an earthworm in the soil with a big question mark over it.

outcomes: I can say what a backbone is, and sort animals into those that have one and those that do not.
I can explain that most animals have no backbone, and show it by counting the animals in one small patch.
I can say how worms, snails, crabs, spiders, insects, starfish and jellyfish hold their shape: with water held tight inside, with a shell, or with armour on the outside.
I can tell an insect from a spider, a crab and a centipede by counting legs and body parts.
I can run a fair test, fill in a table, draw a bar chart, and say what I think, what I saw and why.
I can explain that 'animals without backbones' is not one family. A starfish is a closer cousin of ours than of a snail.
I can say what scientists still do not know about these animals, and how to watch small animals kindly.

terms.meaning: The long chain of small bones down the middle of your back. It holds your body up and protects the soft cord of nerves inside it. Scientists also call it the spine.
terms.example: You can feel your backbone as a row of bumps when you bend forward.
terms.art: A child's back with the bumps of the backbone drawn as a row of small round bones.

terms.meaning: One of the small bones that join together to make a backbone. More than one are called vertebrae.
terms.example: You have 33 vertebrae, stacked like a pile of cotton reels.
terms.art: A stack of small round bones like cotton reels, one of them lifted out and labelled.

terms.meaning: An animal with a backbone. Fish, frogs, snakes, lizards, birds and mammals are vertebrates.
terms.example: A crow, a cat, a fish and you are all vertebrates.
terms.art: A crow, a cat, a fish and a child in a row, each with a thin line showing the backbone inside.

terms.meaning: An animal with no backbone. The word means 'not a vertebrate'. Most animals are invertebrates.
terms.example: An ant, an earthworm and a snail are invertebrates.
terms.art: An ant, an earthworm and a snail in a row, with no line of bones inside them.

terms.meaning: The hard or firm frame that holds an animal's body in shape. It can be inside the body, outside it, or made of water.
terms.example: Your bones are your skeleton. A crab's hard shell is its skeleton.
terms.art: Side by side: a child's bones inside, a crab's shell outside, and a worm full of water.

terms.meaning: A hard skeleton on the outside of the body, like a suit of armour. 'Exo' means outside.
terms.example: A crab, a beetle and a spider all wear an exoskeleton.
terms.art: A beetle with its hard shiny outer case drawn like a knight's armour.

terms.meaning: To crack open and climb out of an old exoskeleton that has become too tight, and then grow a bigger one. Moulting is also how snakes and birds lose old skin and feathers.
terms.example: A crab moults many times as it grows. For a few days its new shell is soft.
terms.art: A crab backing out of its old empty shell, which stays behind like a ghost crab.

terms.meaning: A body held firm by water squeezed tight inside it, like a water balloon. Scientists call it a hydrostatic skeleton.
terms.example: An earthworm stays firm because it is full of liquid held in by its muscles.
terms.art: An earthworm drawn see-through, its rings full of blue liquid, next to a tied water balloon.

terms.meaning: One of the many rings or sections that a body is made of, joined in a row.
terms.example: An earthworm has more than a hundred segments. An ant's leg has segments too.
terms.art: An earthworm with its rings counted, and an ant's leg with its joints marked.

terms.meaning: A soft-bodied animal with no backbone. Many molluscs make a shell. Snails, slugs, clams, octopuses and squid are molluscs.
terms.example: The snail on a wet wall and the octopus in the sea are both molluscs.
terms.art: A snail, a clam shell, a slug and an octopus together on a rock.

terms.meaning: An animal with an exoskeleton and legs that bend at joints. Insects, spiders, crabs, centipedes and millipedes are arthropods.
terms.example: An ant, a spider and a crab are all arthropods.
terms.art: An ant, a spider and a crab with their leg joints circled.

terms.meaning: An arthropod with 6 legs and a body in 3 parts: head, middle and back end. Most insects also have wings and 2 feelers.
terms.example: Ants, bees, flies, mosquitoes, beetles and butterflies are insects.
terms.art: An ant drawn large with its 3 body parts coloured differently and its 6 legs numbered.

terms.meaning: An arthropod with 8 legs and a body in 2 parts, and no feelers. Spiders, scorpions, ticks and mites are arachnids.
terms.example: The spider in the corner of your bathroom is an arachnid, not an insect.
terms.art: A spider drawn large with its 2 body parts coloured and its 8 legs numbered.

terms.meaning: A feeler on the head of an insect or a crab, used to smell, taste and touch. More than one are called antennae.
terms.example: An ant taps its antennae on another ant to smell who it is.
terms.art: Two ants touching antennae, with little smell-wave lines between them.

terms.meaning: A long, bendy arm used to grab, feel or sting. Jellyfish and octopuses have tentacles.
terms.example: A jellyfish's tentacles trail below it like long strings.
terms.art: A jellyfish with long trailing tentacles in blue water.

terms.meaning: Hundreds of tiny soft feet under a starfish's arms. Each one can grip like a small sucker.
terms.example: A starfish walks slowly over rocks on its tube feet.
terms.art: The underside of a starfish arm, with rows of tiny tube feet like little bubbles.

terms.meaning: A tiny cell in a jellyfish's tentacle that shoots out a thread like a harpoon to sting prey.
terms.example: If a tentacle brushes your leg at the beach, thousands of stinging cells fire at once.
terms.art: A zoom-in of a tentacle with tiny coiled threads shooting out.

terms.meaning: When one half or part of a shape matches another. We have two matching sides. A starfish has five matching arms around a middle.
terms.example: Fold a butterfly picture down the middle and the two wings match. Turn a starfish and each arm looks the same.
terms.art: A child with a mirror line down the middle, next to a starfish with five lines from its centre.

terms.meaning: One kind of living thing. Animals of the same species can have babies together.
terms.example: The house sparrow is one species. The common garden ant is another.
terms.art: Three different kinds of ant side by side, each labelled as a different species.

terms.meaning: To grow a lost body part back again. Scientists call it regeneration.
terms.example: A starfish can regrow a lost arm. Some flatworms can regrow a whole body from a small piece.
terms.art: A starfish with four full arms and one small new arm growing back.

explanations.definition: A backbone is a chain of small bones, called vertebrae, that runs down the middle of an animal's back. Animals with a backbone are called vertebrates. Animals without one are called invertebrates.
explanations.description: Your backbone does two jobs. It holds your body up, so you can stand tall and bend. It also protects your spinal cord. That is the soft rope of nerves that carries messages between your brain and your body. Fish, frogs, snakes, lizards, birds and mammals all have a backbone. Worms, snails, crabs, spiders, insects, starfish and jellyfish do not. They have no bones at all.
examples: You can feel your backbone as a row of bumps when you bend forward.
A fish bone left on your plate after dinner is part of the fish's backbone and ribs.
A snake has no legs, but it has a very long backbone, with hundreds of vertebrae.
explanations.art: A cut-away drawing of a child, a fish and a snake, each with its backbone shown in white, next to an earthworm with nothing inside but soft rings.
explanations.context: This card explains the first idea of the unit: what a backbone is, and which animals have one.

explanations.definition: Most kinds of animals are invertebrates. Of all the animal species people have named, about 95 out of every 100 have no backbone.
explanations.description: Scientists have named roughly one and a half million kinds of animal. Only about 70 thousand of them have a backbone. Insects alone make up about one million of the named kinds. Beetles are the biggest group of all. And there are many more invertebrates still waiting to be found and named. They are under stones, in the soil, in the deep sea and on the leaves of rainforests. So when people say 'animal', they often picture a cow or a tiger. But a more honest picture of an animal would be a small beetle.
examples: If you lift a flowerpot, you may find ants, woodlice, a worm and a centipede, but probably no animal with a backbone.

In one small garden in England, a scientist called Jennifer Owen counted the animals for 30 years. She found more than 2,600 kinds of plants and animals. Most of them were insects and other animals without backbones.
A single big tree in a rainforest can hold hundreds of kinds of beetle.
explanations.art: A big pie chart drawn as a cake: one thin slice with a fish, a bird and a cat, and the rest of the cake crowded with beetles, ants, worms, snails, spiders and crabs.
explanations.context: This card explains the big surprise of the unit: animals with a backbone are only a small slice of all animals.

explanations.concept: Bodies held firm by water: worms
explanations.definition: An earthworm has no bones. It stays firm because its body is full of liquid, held tight by muscles in its skin. This is called a water skeleton, or a hydrostatic skeleton.
explanations.description: Think of a long balloon full of water. If you squeeze the middle, the balloon gets longer and thinner. If you push the ends together, it gets shorter and fatter. A worm works the same way. It has two sets of muscles. One set goes round the body like rubber bands. When they squeeze, that part of the worm gets long and thin and pushes forward. The other set runs along the body. When they pull, that part gets short and fat and holds on to the soil. Tiny bristles on each segment grip the soil too. Squeeze, stretch, grip, pull. That is how a worm crawls without a single bone.
examples: Pick up an earthworm gently after rain. It feels firm, not floppy, because of the liquid inside.
If you squeeze a water balloon in your fist, it bulges out between your fingers. The water cannot be squashed, so it moves somewhere else.
A sea anemone and a slug also use water to hold their shape.
explanations.art: A see-through earthworm in three pictures: the front part squeezed long and thin, then the back part pulled short and fat, with tiny bristles gripping the soil.
explanations.context: This card explains how worms stay firm and move without bones. It goes with the Water Bones experiment.

explanations.definition: A snail is a mollusc, a soft-bodied animal with no backbone. Its shell is made by its own body, from the same stuff as chalk.
explanations.description: A snail's shell is not a house it found. It grows with the snail. A thin layer of the snail's body, called the mantle, lines the inside of the shell. The mantle takes chalky stuff from the snail's food and water and adds it to the open edge of the shell. So the shell grows bigger in a spiral, round and round. If the shell cracks, the snail can patch it from the inside. The snail itself is soft and wet. It moves on one big muscly foot, sliding on a layer of slime. Clams, oysters, slugs, octopuses and squid are molluscs too. Slugs and octopuses have lost the outside shell over millions of years.
examples: The spiral on a garden snail's shell shows how it grew, ring after ring, from the tiny tip in the middle.
A pearl is made the same way. An oyster coats a bit of grit with layer after layer of shell stuff.
An octopus is a mollusc with no shell at all, so it can squeeze through a gap as small as its beak.
explanations.art: A snail shell cut in half to show the spiral inside, with the soft snail and its mantle at the open edge adding a new white rim.
explanations.context: This card explains how a snail gets its shell. The snail makes it, and the shell grows with the snail.

explanations.concept: Armour on the outside: crabs, spiders and insects
explanations.definition: Crabs, spiders, insects, centipedes and millipedes are arthropods. They wear a hard skeleton on the outside, called an exoskeleton, and their legs bend at joints.
explanations.description: Your bones are inside, with your muscles wrapped around them. An arthropod is the other way round. Its hard skeleton is outside, and its muscles are inside, pulling on it. The armour is made mostly of a tough material called chitin. In crabs it is also packed with chalky stuff, which makes it extra hard. Each leg is a set of hollow tubes joined at bendy places, like the joints of a straw. The armour protects the animal and stops it drying out. But armour cannot stretch. So to grow, an arthropod must moult. It makes a new soft skin underneath, splits the old one and climbs out. Then it puffs itself up with air or water before the new armour hardens.
examples: An empty cicada or crab shell left on a tree or beach is an old exoskeleton. The animal climbed out of it.
A cockroach's back is hard and shiny because it is armour.
Prawns turn pink when cooked because of the colour stored in their shell.
explanations.art: A crab drawn half see-through: hard red armour outside, pale muscles inside pulling on the shell, and an empty old shell lying beside it.
explanations.context: This card explains exoskeletons, the armour that crabs, spiders and insects wear on the outside.

explanations.concept: Count the legs: insect, spider, crab or centipede?
explanations.definition: Arthropods can be sorted by their legs and body parts. Insects have 6 legs and 3 body parts. Spiders have 8 legs and 2 body parts. Crabs and prawns have 10 legs. Centipedes and millipedes have many legs along a long body.
explanations.description: Here is the quickest way to tell them apart. Count the legs. Six legs means an insect. Look again and you will see three parts: a head, a middle and a back end. Most insects also have wings and two feelers. Eight legs means an arachnid, like a spider or a scorpion. A spider's body has only two parts, and it has no feelers. Ten legs, with two of them often made into big claws, means a crab or a prawn. These live mostly in water and breathe with gills. Lots of legs on a long, ringed body means a centipede or a millipede. A centipede has one pair of legs on each segment and runs fast. A millipede has two pairs on each segment and walks slowly.
examples: An ant has 6 legs, so it is an insect.
A spider has 8 legs, so it is not an insect. It is an arachnid.
A woodlouse, the small grey animal that rolls into a ball, has 14 legs. It is a land cousin of crabs and prawns.
explanations.art: Four animals in a row, ant, spider, crab and centipede, with their legs numbered and their body parts outlined in different colours.
explanations.context: This card explains how to tell an insect, a spider, a crab and a centipede apart by counting legs and body parts.

explanations.concept: Starfish: five arms and no brain
explanations.definition: A starfish is an invertebrate that lives in the sea. It has a body with five matching parts around a middle, hundreds of tube feet, and no brain. Scientists prefer to call it a sea star, because it is not a fish.
explanations.description: Most animals you know have a front and a back, and a left side that matches the right side. A starfish is different. It has five arms around a middle, like the spokes of a wheel. Its mouth is underneath, in the centre. Under each arm are rows of tiny tube feet. They are filled with seawater and can grip like little suckers. The starfish walks on them slowly, and pulls open clam shells with them. It has no brain, just a ring of nerves around its mouth and a nerve down each arm. There is a tiny eye at the tip of each arm that can tell light from dark. If a starfish loses an arm, it can slowly grow a new one.
examples: On rocky beaches in India, like the reef at Narara in Gujarat, you can see sea stars in pools at low tide.
A starfish eats a clam by pushing its own stomach out of its mouth and into the clam's shell.
Sea urchins and sea cucumbers are cousins of the starfish. They also have tube feet and parts in fives.
explanations.art: A starfish turned over to show its mouth in the middle and rows of tiny tube feet along each arm, with one small arm growing back.
explanations.context: This card explains starfish: animals with five matching arms, tube feet and no brain.

explanations.concept: Jellyfish: a body made mostly of water
explanations.definition: A jellyfish is an invertebrate with a soft body that is about 95 parts in 100 water. It has no bones, no brain, no heart and no blood. It catches food with stinging tentacles.
explanations.description: A jellyfish is like a living umbrella of jelly. The sea holds it up. If a jellyfish is washed onto the beach, it collapses into a flat blob, because there is nothing to hold its shape out of water. It swims by squeezing its bell, which pushes water out behind it. Its tentacles hang below, covered in stinging cells. Each stinging cell holds a coiled thread, like a tiny harpoon. When a small fish touches it, the threads fire and the venom stops the fish. Jellyfish have no brain, but they have a net of nerves spread through the whole body. Jellyfish-like animals were swimming in the sea more than 500 million years ago, long before there were dinosaurs or trees.
examples: Never touch a jellyfish on the beach, even one that looks dead. Its stinging cells can still fire.
Corals and sea anemones are close cousins of jellyfish. They have stinging tentacles too.
Some jellyfish glow in the dark sea. The glowing green material from one jellyfish is now used by scientists all over the world to light up cells.
explanations.art: A see-through jellyfish in blue water, its bell squeezing, tentacles trailing, with one tentacle zoomed in to show coiled stinging threads.
explanations.context: This card explains jellyfish: soft animals made mostly of water, held up by the sea.

explanations.definition: Invertebrates are not one family of animals. The word just means 'every animal that is not a vertebrate'. Some invertebrates are more closely related to us than to other invertebrates.
explanations.description: Imagine you sorted all the people in the world into 'my family' and 'everyone else'. 'Everyone else' would not be a family. It would hold many families, some close to yours and some far away. 'Invertebrate' is like that. It holds many very different branches of the animal family tree. Scientists compare the bodies, the way babies grow, and the genes of animals to draw this tree. And it gives a surprise. Starfish and sea urchins are on the same big branch as vertebrates, the branch that includes you. So a starfish is a closer cousin of yours than it is of a snail, a spider or a jellyfish. Jellyfish branched off very early, long before worms or snails.
examples: A starfish and a fish share a branch. A starfish and a jellyfish do not, even though both live in the sea and have no bones.
An octopus is closer to a snail than to a fish, even though it swims like a fish.
A woodlouse lives on land, but it is a cousin of crabs and prawns.
explanations.art: A simple branching tree: jellyfish on a low early branch, then a split, with worms, snails, insects, spiders and crabs on one side, and starfish, fish, birds and a child on the other.
explanations.context: This card explains that 'animals without backbones' is not a real family. It is everything except one branch.

explanations.description: Most invertebrates on land are small. The biggest land insects today are only about as long as your hand. But about 300 million years ago, there were giant dragonfly-like insects with wings about 70 centimetres across. That is more than two school rulers laid end to end. Why are there no giant ants today? Scientists are not sure. They have a few ideas, and they argue about which matters most.
examples: Meganeura, a giant dragonfly-like insect that lived about 300 million years ago, had wings about 70 cm across. Its fossils were found in France.
In the sea, where water holds up heavy bodies, some invertebrates are huge. The giant squid can be longer than a bus.
The Japanese spider crab has legs that can stretch about 3.7 metres from tip to tip.

perspectives.explanation: Insects breathe through tiny tubes that run through their bodies. Air does not travel far down thin tubes. When the air had more oxygen, about 300 million years ago, the air could reach deeper, so insects could be bigger. Experiments show some insects raised in extra oxygen grow a little bigger.

Armour gets very heavy as an animal gets bigger. And every moult leaves the animal soft and helpless for a while. A giant soft ant would be squashed by its own weight, or eaten. So armour itself may keep land invertebrates small.
When birds and, later, bats appeared, big flying insects may have been easy food. Giant insects may have disappeared because new hunters arrived, not only because the air changed.

explanations.art: A modern dragonfly next to the shadow of a giant ancient one with a 70 cm wingspan, and a school ruler drawn underneath for size.
explanations.context: This card is about a question scientists still argue about: why most animals without backbones are small.

explanations.concept: Shells, chalk and marble: invertebrates build the Earth
explanations.definition: Many invertebrates build shells and skeletons from calcium carbonate, the same material as chalk and limestone. Over millions of years their remains pile up and turn into rock.
explanations.description: When a snail makes its shell, it uses tiny pieces of calcium, carbon and oxygen, joined together. Corals, clams and many tiny sea creatures do the same. When they die, their shells and skeletons sink and pile up on the sea floor, layer on layer. Over millions of years the layers are pressed into limestone rock. If limestone is squeezed and heated deep underground, it can turn into marble. So many of the white stones people build with began as the bodies of sea animals. Worms change the Earth too. Charles Darwin spent about 40 years studying earthworms. He showed that they slowly bury stones and old buildings by pulling leaves down and pushing soil up.
examples: Limestone rocks in the Himalaya and in the caves of Meghalaya hold fossil shells from ancient seas.
Marble is limestone that was heated and squeezed deep underground. Much limestone began as the shells and skeletons of sea creatures.
Coral reefs, like those near the Andaman Islands and Lakshadweep, are giant stone structures built by tiny animals related to jellyfish.
explanations.art: A cut-away of the sea floor: living snails and corals at the top, old shells piling up below, then layers of pale rock, and at the bottom a block of white marble.
explanations.context: This card follows the idea out to the Earth itself: how shells built by animals without backbones become rock.

explanations.concept: Tiny and tough: tardigrades and the first animals
explanations.definition: The first animals on Earth were invertebrates. Some invertebrates alive today, like tardigrades, can survive things no other animal can, even the empty space outside Earth.
explanations.description: For most of the history of animals, there were no backbones at all. The first animals lived in the sea more than 550 million years ago, and they were all soft invertebrates. Backbones came later. Today there is a tiny invertebrate called a tardigrade, or water bear. It is smaller than a grain of sand, with 8 stubby legs. It lives in damp moss, even on walls and roofs in Indian towns. When its home dries out, it curls up, dries out too and waits. In 2007, scientists sent dried tardigrades into space outside a spacecraft. Many came back alive and later had babies. They were the first animals known to survive open space.
examples: Tardigrades can be found in damp moss from a wall, looked at with a microscope.
Trilobites were armoured sea invertebrates that lived for about 270 million years and then all died out.
Sponges are invertebrates so simple that they have no muscles or nerves at all.
explanations.art: A plump, eight-legged tardigrade drawn huge on a moss leaf, with a small spacecraft and stars in a round window behind it.
explanations.context: This card follows invertebrates out to deep time and to space: the first animals, and the toughest.

explanations.description: All animals share one ancestor, which lived in the sea long ago. Scientists agree on that. But they still argue about which living group branched off the animal family tree first. Was it the sponges, simple animals with no nerves or muscles? Or was it the comb jellies, see-through sea animals that do have nerves and muscles? The answer matters. It tells us whether nerves and muscles were invented once, or more than once.
examples: Sponges filter food out of seawater through tiny holes. Bath sponges were once real animals.
Comb jellies swim with rows of tiny beating hairs that flash rainbow colours in light.
Both are invertebrates, and both are older branches than worms, snails or insects.

perspectives.explanation: Sponges are the simplest animals. They have no nerves or muscles. So it makes sense that they branched off first, before nerves and muscles appeared. Some studies of genes agree.
Several large studies of genes put comb jellies at the very bottom of the tree. If they are right, then nerves and muscles may have appeared twice, or sponges lost theirs.

explanations.art: A branching tree with a question mark at the very bottom, a sponge on one side and a rainbow-lit comb jelly on the other.
explanations.context: This card is about an open argument: which animal group is the oldest branch of the family tree.

explanations.description: Animals without backbones feel. A worm pulls back from a sharp stick. A crab rubs and guards a hurt leg. An octopus stays away from a place where it was once hurt. Every living thing senses the world and responds to it, with a backbone or without one. For a long time, many people said small animals felt nothing. In 2022, a law in the United Kingdom began to count crabs, lobsters, octopuses and squid as animals that feel.
examples: In experiments, hermit crabs given a small electric shock in their shell were later more likely to leave that shell for a new one. This suggests something more than a reflex.
An octopus that is hurt will guard and clean the hurt place.
We do not know what it is like to be an ant. That is one of the hardest questions in science.

perspectives.who: Many scientists who study crabs and octopuses
perspectives.explanation: Crabs and octopuses act as if they feel pain. They learn to avoid places where they were hurt, and they guard hurt parts. So we should treat them as if they can feel.
These animals may just have clever reflexes and learning, with no feeling at all. Feeling may need a brain built like ours. We cannot yet tell from the outside.

explanations.art: A hermit crab peeking out of its shell, a child crouched at a kind distance, and a question mark floating between them.
explanations.context: This card is about a question scientists still argue about: whether animals without backbones can feel pain. It is why we handle small animals gently.

agreed.text: Most kinds of animal have no backbone.
agreed.evidence: Scientists have named about one and a half million animal species. Only about 70 thousand of them are vertebrates. Insects alone are about one million.
agreed.context: This card is about what scientists agree on: most animals are invertebrates.

agreed.text: Animals without backbones hold their shape in different ways: water held tight inside, a shell, or armour on the outside.
agreed.evidence: Cut a worm's body open in pictures and you find liquid, not bone. A crab's shell comes off whole when it moults. A snail's shell grows with the snail.
agreed.context: This card is about what scientists agree on: how boneless animals hold their shape.

agreed.text: Insects have 6 legs and spiders have 8. Spiders are not insects.
agreed.evidence: Every adult insect ever studied has 6 legs on its middle part. Every spider has 8 legs and no feelers.
agreed.context: This card is about what scientists agree on: spiders and insects are different groups.

agreed.evidence: People have watched crabs, insects and spiders climb out of old skins thousands of times. The empty skins can be collected and measured.
agreed.context: This card is about what scientists agree on: animals with armour grow by moulting.

agreed.text: 'Invertebrate' is not one family. Starfish are closer cousins of vertebrates than of snails or insects.
agreed.evidence: The way starfish babies grow in the egg is like ours, and different from snails and insects. Studies of genes show the same thing.
agreed.context: This card is about what scientists agree on: invertebrates are many different families.

challenging.claim: Worms, insects and other small animals grow by themselves out of mud, rotting meat or old cloth.
challenging.who: Many people for thousands of years, including the Greek thinker Aristotle.
challenging.for: Maggots really do appear on meat left out, and worms appear after rain. Nobody saw where they came from.
challenging.against: In 1668 an Italian doctor, Francesco Redi, put meat in jars. Some jars were open and some were covered with cloth. Maggots appeared only on the meat that flies could reach. Flies had laid tiny eggs.
challenging.context: This card is about an old idea of where small animals come from, and the experiment that ended it.

challenging.claim: Animals without backbones are simple, lower animals, and backboned animals are higher and better.
challenging.who: A very common idea, found in old books that drew animals on a ladder with humans at the top.
challenging.for: Many invertebrates are small, and some, like sponges, are very simple.
challenging.against: Life is a branching tree, not a ladder. Every animal alive today has had exactly as long to change as we have. An octopus can solve puzzles. Bees can learn shapes. Some invertebrates have more genes than we do.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that invertebrates are 'lower' animals, and why scientists have dropped it.

challenging.who: Many people, and even some old dictionaries.
challenging.for: Spiders are small, have legs and hard skins, and live in the same places as insects.
challenging.against: Spiders have 8 legs, 2 body parts and no feelers. Insects have 6 legs, 3 body parts and feelers. Spiders are arachnids, cousins of scorpions and mites.
challenging.context: This card is about a very common mix-up: spiders are not insects.

challenging.claim: Invertebrates cannot feel anything. They are like little machines.
challenging.who: The French thinker René Descartes, about 380 years ago, said this about all animals. Many people still think it about insects.
challenging.for: Many invertebrates have small nerve systems. Some of their actions are simple reflexes.
challenging.against: Crabs and octopuses learn to avoid places where they were hurt and guard hurt parts. In 2022 the United Kingdom's law began counting them as animals that can feel.
challenging.context: This card is about the old idea that small animals feel nothing, and why scientists now argue about it.

challenging.claim: If you cut an earthworm in two, you get two worms.
challenging.who: A very common belief among children and grown-ups.
challenging.for: Some worms really can regrow. A flatworm called a planarian can grow a whole new body from a small piece.
challenging.against: An earthworm cut in two usually dies. Sometimes the front part, with the head, can grow a new tail if the cut is near the back. The back part cannot grow a new head. So you never get two worms.
challenging.context: This card is about a common belief about cutting worms, and what really happens.

challenging.claim: There may be several million kinds of animal still not discovered, nearly all of them invertebrates.
challenging.who: Several groups of scientists who study how many species there are.
challenging.for: New insects, worms and sea animals are named every year, thousands of them. Whole places, like the deep sea floor, are hardly explored.
challenging.against: Other scientists think the number is smaller, perhaps a few million. Estimates differ a lot, because we are guessing about animals nobody has seen.
challenging.context: This card is about how many kinds of animal might still be waiting to be found.

big_questions.q: If an ant could name all the animals, would it call us 'the animals with no armour'? Who decides what is normal?
big_questions.hint: We named animals by comparing them to ourselves. What would an ant compare us to?

big_questions.q: How can a worm push through hard soil with no bones at all?
big_questions.hint: Squeeze the middle of a water balloon. Which way does the water go?

big_questions.q: Why does a crab have to break out of its own armour to grow?
big_questions.hint: Can a steel tumbler grow bigger? What would you do if your clothes could not stretch?

big_questions.q: Is a worm less important than a tiger? What would happen to a forest without worms?
big_questions.hint: Think about where fallen leaves go, and who mixes the soil.

big_questions.q: A starfish has no brain. How does it know where to go?
big_questions.hint: Can your hand pull away from a hot pan before you have even thought about it?

big_questions.q: Most animals on Earth are small and boneless. What does that tell us about what life is good at?
big_questions.hint: Count how many places a tiny animal can live that a big one cannot.

big_questions.q: Why do you think the first animals had no bones?
big_questions.hint: What would an animal need before it could build bones? Where did the first animals live?

big_questions.q: Is it fair to squash an ant just because it is small? What about a mosquito that bites?
big_questions.hint: There is no single right answer. What reasons would you give either way?

big_questions.q: If a jellyfish has no brain, can it be awake or asleep?
big_questions.hint: Scientists found that one kind of jellyfish does something like sleeping at night. What could sleep be for?

big_questions.q: A starfish is a closer cousin of yours than a snail is. How does that change the way you look at a starfish?
big_questions.hint: Who are your cousins? Do cousins have to look like you?

story.title: The Shell Nobody Lent
story.note: Jeanne Villepreux-Power is real (1794 to 1871). She grew up poor in a French village, became a dressmaker in Paris, married James Power and moved to Messina in Sicily. Around 1832 she built glass tanks and sea cages to keep sea animals alive and watch them. She showed that the argonaut, a small octopus, makes and mends its own shell. Many of her notes were later lost in a shipwreck. Rosa, her father and the cracked shell in this story are imagined.
text: The summer I was nine, a lady from France began buying the worst of my father's catch.

My father was a fisherman in Messina, a harbour town on the island of Sicily. Most mornings he sold his fish in the market. But some mornings his net came up with things nobody would eat. Spiky sea urchins. Starfish, stiff and orange. Jellyfish that slid off the boat like spilled soup. And sometimes, a paper sailor.

A paper sailor is a small octopus that lives inside a shell. The shell is white and as thin as an eggshell, curled like a ram's horn. When you hold it up to the sun, the light shines through it. The fishermen thought it was lucky. The learned men of the town thought it was a thief.

"It finds an empty shell left by some other creature," the doctor told my father, "and it climbs inside, like a hermit crab. A soft thing like that, with no bones in its body, could never make something hard."
My father nodded, because the doctor had books. I nodded too.

The French lady was called Signora Power. She did not nod. She had a sharp chin and quick, sewing fingers. People said she had once been a poor girl in a village far away, and had walked most of the way to Paris to find work. There she had sewn dresses so fine that a princess wore one at her wedding. Now she was married to an English merchant, and she spent her days on the rocks with her skirts tied up, staring into pools.
"Has anyone seen it?" she asked my father. "Has anyone actually watched a paper sailor take a shell that was not its own?"
Nobody had. Nobody had watched a paper sailor do anything. Out of the sea, they died in an hour.

So Signora Power built boxes of glass. She was the first person anyone had heard of to keep sea animals alive in glass and watch them. When the glass boxes were too small, she built big wooden cages and lowered them into the harbour on ropes, so the sea itself flowed through them. Then she paid me one coin for every paper sailor I brought her alive, in a bucket of seawater, running.
I ran a great deal that summer.

I learned to sit with her on the stone steps above the cages. I learned to be still. I learned that a starfish moves on hundreds of tiny wet feet, so slowly that you have to look away and look back to see it has moved. I learned that a sea urchin's spines are all on the outside, like a fort with no one inside. I learned that the paper sailor holds its shell with two broad arms, spread over the outside of the shell like hands over a cup.
"Why does she hold it like that?" I asked.
"That," said Signora Power, "is the question."
Then, in late summer, I did something terrible.

I was lifting a bucket onto the steps when my foot slipped on the green weed. The bucket tipped. The paper sailor inside it struck the stone. When I scooped her back into the water, there was a crack across the edge of her shell, and a piece the size of my thumbnail was gone.

I cried all the way to the cages. I was sure she would die, or the Signora would send me away. The Signora did neither. She took the paper sailor from me very gently and lowered her into the smallest cage.
"Now we will see," she said. "A thief would have to go and steal another shell. Let us see what she does."
The next morning I was on the steps before the sun.

The paper sailor had not left her shell. She had spread her two broad arms over the broken edge, and held them there, pressed close. All that day she held them there. And the next day. On the third morning the Signora called me, and her voice was strange.
"Rosa. Look."

Across the hole, where the piece had broken away, there was a thin white film. It was like the skin that forms on boiled milk. Over the next days it grew thicker and whiter. It went cloudy, then pale, then hard. By the end of the week the hole was gone. There was only a faint line, like a mended seam in a dress.
Signora Power looked at that line for a long time.
"She made it," she said at last. "Out of the sea. With her own arms. Nobody lent her this shell."

She wrote it all down that night in her careful hand. Later, she showed the mended shells to scientists from many countries. Some of them did not believe a dressmaker. But the shells were there to see, and so was the line.

I am old now. I have mended many nets and a few hearts. Sometimes, when my back aches, I run my fingers down the bumps of my own backbone. My hard parts are on the inside. The paper sailor's are on the outside. A crab's armour, a snail's spiral, the chalky spines of an urchin, all of them were made, grain by grain, by soft bodies out of what they ate and the water around them.
So were mine.

I think of the doctor, who had books, and of the lady who had a bucket and a summer and the patience to look. And I think of that thin white film, spreading across a broken place, in the dark green water of the harbour.
story.epiphany: For the parent: people thought a soft animal with no bones could never make something hard, so the argonaut must have stolen its shell. Watching proved them wrong. Animals without backbones build their hard parts too, as shells and armour on the outside, made from what they eat and the water around them. Snails, crabs, corals and the argonaut all do it. Our bones are made the same way, from food, only on the inside. The story also asks who gets believed: the man with books, or the woman who watched.
ask: Why did the doctor think the paper sailor must have stolen its shell?
How did the cracked shell help Signora Power find the answer?
Your bones are inside. The paper sailor's shell is outside. Where did each of them come from?
Why do you think some scientists did not believe Signora Power at first?
What would you like to watch for a whole summer, to find out something nobody knows?

games.title: Backbone or Not?
games.players: 2 to 5 players, or one child playing against the app
games.context: This is a card game about which animals have a backbone and which do not. A backbone is the chain of small bones down the middle of your back. Some cards are tricks, like the starfish, which is not a fish.

printables.title: 30 animal cards to cut out, each with a picture and a name
Two playing mats
items: BACKBONE: a chain of bones inside
NO BACKBONE: water, shell or armour

printables.title: Tally sheet: how many cards on each mat

rules: Cut out the 30 cards. Shuffle them and put them face down in a pile.
On your turn, take the top card and read the animal's name out loud.
Put it on the BACKBONE mat or the NO BACKBONE mat. Say one reason, like 'it has a shell' or 'it has bones like a fish'.
If you are right and give a reason, take a bone token. Check the answer list on the back of the tally sheet.
Trick cards, like the starfish, seahorse, silverfish and cuttlefish, win two tokens if you get them right and say why.
When all the cards are played, count the cards on each mat. Then the player with most tokens wins.

setup.art: Two paper mats on the floor, one with a drawing of a fish skeleton and one with a drawing of a snail shell and a crab, and a pile of face-down animal cards.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out the two mats. Put the cards face down in a pile.

setup.art: A child holding up a starfish card, looking puzzled, with both mats in front of her.
setup.caption: 2. Take a card. Decide which mat it goes on, and say why.

setup.art: Two tall stacks of cards: a small pile on the backbone mat and a much bigger pile on the no-backbone mat.
setup.caption: 3. At the end, count the cards on each mat.

flow.do: 1. Lay the two mats on the floor. 2. Shuffle the 30 cards and put them face down. 3. Put the bone tokens in a bowl.
flow.say: A backbone is the chain of small bones down the middle of your back. Each card is an animal. We will decide together: does it have a backbone, or not?
flow.kid: Put the two mats down. Mix the cards. Put them face down. For each animal, decide. Does it have a backbone, or not?
flow.context: This is the first step of Backbone or Not?, a card game about which animals have a backbone. Here you set up the game.

flow.do: Find the Earthworm card. Play it together as a practice round.
flow.say: Let's practise with one card. An earthworm. Does it have a backbone?
flow.kid: Practice card: an earthworm. Backbone or not? Tap your answer.

ask.q: How does a worm stay firm with no bones?
good: Its muscles squeeze the liquid inside it.

check.q: An earthworm. Which mat does it go on?
check.why: An earthworm has no bones at all. It stays firm because it is full of liquid held tight by its muscles. Picking BACKBONE often happens because the worm is long and bendy, like a snake. But a snake has a backbone inside, and a worm has none.

flow.do: Take turns drawing cards and placing them. Help with the trick cards: starfish, jellyfish, seahorse, silverfish, cuttlefish and sea cucumber.
flow.say: Watch out for tricky ones. A name can fool you. A starfish is not a fish. A seahorse is a fish. Look at the animal, not just its name.
flow.kid: Take a card. Put it on a mat. Say why. Watch out: some names are tricks!
flow.parent: The trick cards: starfish, jellyfish, cuttlefish and silverfish have no backbone, even though their names say fish. A seahorse is a real fish with a backbone. Sea cucumbers are cousins of starfish, with no backbone. The bat has a backbone, like all mammals. The cobra has a backbone, though it has no legs.

check.why: A seahorse is a real fish. It has a backbone and breathes with gills. Picking NO BACKBONE usually means the curly shape and the name 'horse' fooled you. Look for bones, fins and gills, not the name.

flow.do: When all the cards are placed, count the cards on each mat and write the two numbers on the tally sheet.
flow.say: Let's count. How many cards on the backbone mat? How many on the no backbone mat?
flow.kid: Count the cards on each mat. Write the two numbers down.
flow.think: Our card game has more backbone animals than real life. In the real world, out of every 100 kinds of animal, about 95 have no backbone. Why do you think the game has so many backbone animals?
flow.parent: The answer list. With a backbone: cow, sparrow, cobra, gecko, frog, rohu, seahorse, bat and tortoise. Every other card has no backbone. That is 9 cards with a backbone and 21 without. The game has more backbone animals than real life, because people know them better. That is worth talking about.

flow.do: Ask your child to say three things: what I think, what I saw, and why.
flow.say: Let's finish like scientists. What do you think now? What did the cards show? And why do you think so many animals have no backbone?
flow.kid: Finish like a scientist. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: most animals have no backbone. What I saw: 21 of our 30 cards had no backbone. Why: lots of small animals hold themselves up with shells, armour or water instead of bones.

games.title: Guess My Minibeast
games.context: This is a guessing game about small animals without backbones. One player picks a secret animal. The others ask yes or no questions about its legs, shell and body to find it.

printables.title: 12 minibeast cards, each with a picture, a name and its leg count
items: Centipede: many legs, one pair on each segment
Millipede: many legs, two pairs on each segment
Garden snail: no legs, one foot

printables.title: Question helper sheet
items: Does it have more than 6 legs?

rules: Lay all 12 cards face up so everyone can see them.
One player secretly picks one animal and writes its name on a scrap of paper.
The others take turns asking yes or no questions about its body. 'Is it cute?' does not count.
After each answer, turn over every card that it rules out.
Whoever names the secret animal first wins that round and picks the next secret animal.
Try to find the animal in 4 questions or fewer.
