flow.do: 1. Lay out the 12 cards face up. 2. You pick the first secret animal: choose the house spider. Write it on paper.
flow.say: I have picked a secret animal from these cards. Ask me yes or no questions about its body. Try to find it in four questions.
flow.kid: The app has picked a secret animal. Ask yes or no questions about its body. Can you find it in four?
flow.context: This is the first step of Guess My Minibeast. You find a secret small animal by asking about its legs, shell and body.

flow.do: Answer your child's questions truthfully about the house spider. Turn over the cards each answer rules out.
flow.say: Good question. Let's turn over every card that does not fit.
flow.kid: Ask a question. Turn over the cards that do not fit.

ask.q: Which question rules out the most cards?
good: Does it have more than 6 legs?

check.q: The secret animal has more than 6 legs, but no shell like a crab, and lives on land. It has no feelers and 2 body parts. What is it most likely to be?
check.why: A house spider has 8 legs, 2 body parts and no feelers. Picking the ant usually means thinking every small crawling animal is an insect. But an ant has 6 legs and 3 body parts. A prawn has 10 legs and lives in water.

flow.do: Now take turns. Each player picks a secret animal while the others guess.
flow.say: Your turn to pick a secret animal. We will ask the questions.
flow.kid: Your turn. Pick a secret animal. Answer the questions truthfully.
flow.parent: Watch whether your child asks about legs first. Leg count splits the cards fastest. If they ask 'is it brown?', ask them whether that is about its body plan or just its colour.

flow.do: Talk about which questions were the best.
flow.say: Which questions worked best? Why do you think scientists sort minibeasts by counting legs, and not by colour?
flow.kid: Which question was best? Why do legs help more than colour?

check.q: Why do scientists count legs to sort small animals, and not use colour?
options: Colour is too hard to see
The number of legs stays the same in every animal of a group, but colour can change
check.why: Every adult insect has 6 legs and every spider has 8, whatever colour they are. Colours change a lot, even inside one species. Picking 'too hard to see' is a fair worry, but the real reason is that leg number tells you the group.

flow.think: A woodlouse has 14 legs. Which other animals on the cards do you think it is a cousin of?

worksheets.title: Backbone Detective (core)

items.p: What is a backbone?
opts: A hard shell on an animal's back
A chain of small bones down the middle of the back
A long muscle in the back
The skin on an animal's back
items.why: A backbone is a chain of small bones called vertebrae. You can feel it as bumps when you bend forward. Picking 'a hard shell' mixes it up with a crab or snail, whose hard parts are on the outside.
items.art: A child's back with the bumps of the backbone drawn as small round bones.

items.p: Which of these animals has NO backbone?
items.why: An earthworm has no bones at all. Sparrows, frogs and cobras are vertebrates. Picking the cobra usually happens because snakes are long and legless like worms. But a snake has a very long backbone inside.

items.p: An animal with no backbone is called an ____.
items.why: 'Invertebrate' means 'not a vertebrate'. Vertebrates are animals with a backbone.

items.p: Sort these animals. Do they have a backbone or not?
items.why: Fish, lizards and mammals have backbones. Ants, snails, jellyfish, crabs and starfish do not, even though the starfish and jellyfish have 'fish' in their names.

items.p: Match each animal to how it holds its shape.
items.why: Animals without backbones hold their shape in different ways. Worms use water, snails grow a shell, crabs wear armour, and jellyfish are held up by the water around them.

items.p: How many legs does an insect have?
items.why: Every adult insect has 6 legs. Picking 8 is the most common mistake. That is a spider, and spiders are not insects.

items.p: A spider has 8 legs, 2 body parts and no feelers. What is it?
items.why: Spiders are arachnids, like scorpions and mites. Picking 'insect' is a common mix-up, because spiders are small and catch insects. But insects have 6 legs and 3 body parts.

items.p: A starfish is a kind of fish.
items.why: False. A starfish has no backbone, no fins and no gills like a fish. Scientists often call it a sea star instead.

items.p: Most kinds of animal in the world have no backbone.
items.why: True. About 95 out of every 100 named kinds of animal are invertebrates. Insects alone are about one million kinds.

items.p: A crab's hard shell is called an exoskeleton. What does 'exo' mean?
items.why: 'Exo' means outside. An exoskeleton is a skeleton on the outside, like armour. Picking 'inside' mixes it up with our own skeleton, which is inside our body.

items.p: Why must a crab moult?
opts: Its armour cannot stretch, so it must climb out to grow
items.why: Hard armour cannot grow. So a crab makes a new soft skin underneath, splits the old shell and climbs out. Picking 'because it is old' is a guess many people make, but young crabs moult most often, because they grow fastest.

items.p: Remember the Water Bones experiment? You filled long balloons with a little water, half full, and full and tight, and measured how much each drooped over a table edge. Which balloon drooped the least?
opts: The one with a little water
items.why: The full, tight balloon was the firmest, so it drooped least. Water packed in tight pushes out on every side and holds the shape. That is how a worm stays firm. Picking 'a little water' usually means thinking floppy things are stronger.
items.context: Remember the Water Bones experiment? You filled long balloons with a little water, half full, and full and tight, and measured how much each drooped over a table edge.

items.p: How does an earthworm stay firm without any bones? Use the words water and muscles.
items.a: An earthworm is full of water and liquid. Its muscles squeeze the liquid tight, so its body stays firm, like a full water balloon.
items.why: This is called a water skeleton. Squeezing the liquid also lets the worm stretch and push forward.

items.p: Draw an ant. Show its 3 body parts and 6 legs. Label the head.
items.a: A head with two feelers, a middle part with all 6 legs attached, and a back end.
items.why: An insect's 6 legs all join onto its middle part. The feelers are on the head.
items.art: A blank box with the word 'ant' and a small magnifying glass in the corner.

items.p: Remember the Backbone Census, where you counted animals in one small patch. Which group had more kinds? Write one sentence about what you saw and one about why.
items.a: We found more kinds of animal without a backbone. I think this is because small animals can live under stones, in the soil and on leaves, and there are many of those places.
items.why: Most people find many more kinds of invertebrate. It is the same all over the world.
items.context: Remember the Backbone Census? You counted the kinds of animal in one small patch, and sorted them into animals with a backbone and without one.

worksheets.context: This worksheet checks the main ideas: what a backbone is, which animals have one, and how animals without one hold their shape.

worksheets.title: Shells, Armour and Water (stretch)

items.p: Which animal is a mollusc?
items.why: Molluscs are soft-bodied animals, and many of them make shells. Snails, slugs, clams and octopuses are molluscs. Picking the spider mixes up soft bodies with armour. Spiders are arthropods.

items.p: An octopus has no shell, but it is still a mollusc. Which animal is its closest cousin?
items.why: Octopuses and snails are both molluscs. Over millions of years, the octopus family lost the outside shell. Picking the fish is a common guess, because octopuses swim in the sea like fish. But fish have backbones.

items.p: A woodlouse has 14 legs and lives under stones on land. Who are its closest cousins?
items.why: Woodlice are crustaceans, the group with crabs and prawns. They are one of the few crustaceans that live on land. Picking 'insects' is a natural guess, because they are small and live in the same places as ants.

items.p: Put these animals in order, from fewest legs to most legs: spider, ant, crab, earthworm.
items.why: Earthworm 0, ant 6, spider 8, crab 10.

items.p: How does a snail get its shell?
opts: Its body makes it and adds to it as it grows
It is born with a full-size shell
items.why: A snail's mantle, a thin layer of its body, makes the shell from chalky stuff and adds to the open edge as it grows. Picking 'finds an empty one' mixes it up with hermit crabs, which really do borrow shells.

items.p: Match each starfish part to what it does.
items.why: A starfish has no brain. A ring of nerves around its mouth and a nerve in each arm carry its messages.

items.p: A jellyfish washed up on a beach looks like a flat blob. Why?
opts: It has no skeleton, and the sea is no longer holding it up
It has turned into a different animal
items.why: A jellyfish is mostly water, with no bones or armour. In the sea, the water holds its shape. Out of water it collapses. Picking 'broken bones' mixes jellyfish up with fish. Jellyfish have no bones at all.

items.p: If you cut an earthworm in two, you always get two worms.
items.why: False. An earthworm cut in two usually dies. Sometimes the front part can grow a new tail. The back part cannot grow a new head.

items.p: Remember the Armour Tubes experiment? You made a round tube, a square tube and a zigzag from paper, and added notebooks on top until each one crumpled. Which shape held the most?
items.why: The round tube held the most. A tube spreads the weight evenly all the way round, so it is strong without being heavy. Insect and crab legs are tubes of armour for the same reason.
items.context: Remember the Armour Tubes experiment? You made a round tube, a square tube and a zigzag from paper, and added notebooks on top until each one crumpled.

chart.title: Made-up example: how many notebooks each paper shape held

items.p: Remember the Many Small Suckers experiment? You hung a bag from rubber suckers on a tile and added cups of rice until they popped off. One sucker held 3 cups and four suckers held 11 cups. What does that show about a starfish's tube feet?
opts: Small grips add up to a strong hold
Only one tube foot works at a time
Tube feet are made of rubber
items.why: Each tube foot grips only a little, but hundreds of them together hold very tightly. Picking 'only one at a time' would mean four suckers held the same as one, but they held much more.
items.context: Remember the Many Small Suckers experiment? You hung a bag from rubber suckers on a tile and added cups of rice until they popped off.

items.p: Which of these is NOT an arthropod?
items.why: Arthropods have jointed legs and an exoskeleton. A snail has no legs at all. It is a mollusc. Picking the prawn or scorpion usually means forgetting that arthropods include animals from water and animals with stings.

items.p: A millipede has ____ pairs of legs on each segment, and a centipede has ____ pair.
items.why: Millipedes have two pairs on most segments and walk slowly. Centipedes have one pair on each segment and run fast.

items.p: Your bones grow with you, but a crab's armour does not. Why do you think that is?
items.a: My bones are alive inside me, with blood in them, so they can grow. A crab's armour is a hard outer layer that cannot stretch or grow, so the crab has to make a new one.
items.why: Bones are living tissue that grows. An exoskeleton is a hardened outer layer, so it must be shed.

items.p: Draw a starfish from underneath. Show its mouth and the tube feet on each arm.
items.a: Five arms around a middle, a mouth in the centre, and rows of small dots or bubbles along each arm for tube feet.
items.why: A starfish's mouth is in the middle of its underside, and its tube feet run in grooves along each arm.

items.p: Which animal moves by squeezing waves of muscle along one big foot?
items.why: A snail glides on waves of muscle along its one foot, sliding on slime. You can see the waves from underneath through clear plastic. Picking an animal with legs means thinking every crawling animal walks with legs.

worksheets.context: This worksheet goes further: molluscs, arthropods, starfish and jellyfish, and what our experiments showed.

worksheets.title: The Great Family Tree (challenge)

items.p: A starfish and a snail both have no backbone. Which one is a closer cousin of yours?
opts: Both are closer to you than a fish
items.why: Starfish and sea urchins are on the same big branch of the animal family tree as vertebrates. Snails are on a different branch. Picking 'equally far' is the natural guess, because both have no backbone. But 'no backbone' is not a family. It is everything outside our branch.

items.p: Some people say 'invertebrate' is not a real group of animals. What do they mean? Use an example.
items.a: They mean that 'invertebrate' just means 'not a vertebrate'. It is like sorting people into 'my family' and 'everyone else'. For example, a starfish is a closer cousin of ours than of a snail, but both are called invertebrates.
items.why: A real group of animals shares one ancestor that no outsider shares. Invertebrates include many separate branches.

items.p: About 300 million years ago there were giant insects with wings about 70 cm across. Which idea do some scientists use to explain why insects could be so big then?
opts: There was more oxygen in the air then
items.why: One idea is that air had more oxygen then, so oxygen could reach deeper through the tubes that insects breathe with. Other scientists think armour weight or new hunters like birds mattered more. Picking 'backbones' would mean they were not insects. No insect has ever had a backbone.

items.p: Many white stones, like marble, began as something alive. What?
opts: Shells and skeletons of sea animals, pressed into limestone
items.why: Many sea animals build shells from calcium carbonate. Their remains pile up and turn into limestone. Limestone heated and squeezed underground can become marble. Picking 'old trees' mixes it up with coal, which formed from ancient plants.

items.p: Charles Darwin spent about 40 years studying earthworms. Why do you think he thought they were so important? Use what you saw in the Bottle Wormery.
items.a: Worms mix the soil and pull leaves underground. In the wormery the stripes of soil and sand got mixed up and leaves were pulled down. This lets air and water into the soil and makes food for plants.
items.why: Darwin showed worms slowly turn over huge amounts of soil, burying stones and old buildings.
items.context: Remember the Bottle Wormery? You made stripes of soil and sand in a bottle, added earthworms and watched for 14 days.

items.p: A tardigrade is a tiny invertebrate. What did scientists find when they sent dried tardigrades into space?
opts: Many survived and later had babies
items.why: In 2007 dried tardigrades spent days outside a spacecraft. Many came back alive and later laid eggs. They were the first animals known to survive open space. Picking 'grew backbones' is impossible. No animal can grow a backbone in its lifetime.

items.p: Four suckers held 11 cups of rice, but one sucker held 3. Why might four not hold exactly 12?
opts: Some suckers may be pressed on less well, or pulled at an angle, so they do not share the load equally
items.why: In a real test, things are never perfect. One sucker may pop first because it is pulled harder or stuck less well, and then the rest go too. Picking 'stronger together' would give more than 12, not less.
items.context: Remember the Many Small Suckers experiment? You hung a bag from rubber suckers on a tile and added cups of rice until they popped off.

items.p: Scientists all agree that crabs and octopuses feel pain exactly as we do.
items.why: False. Crabs and octopuses act as if they feel pain, and some laws now protect them. But scientists still argue about what, if anything, they feel. We cannot yet tell from the outside.

items.p: In 1668 Francesco Redi put meat in open jars and in jars covered with cloth. Maggots appeared only on the meat in the open jars. What did this show?
opts: Maggots grow from meat by themselves
Maggots come from eggs laid by flies
Meat goes bad only in open jars
items.why: Flies could reach only the open jars, and only those got maggots. So maggots hatch from fly eggs. Picking 'grow from meat by themselves' was the old idea his experiment ended.

items.p: Which is the best question to add to a key so that it separates a spider from a scorpion?
opts: Does it have a long tail with a sting?
items.why: Spiders and scorpions both have 8 legs and live on land, so those questions do not split them. A scorpion has a long tail with a sting and big pincers. Picking '8 legs' is a good question for finding arachnids, but it does not split these two.

items.p: A jellyfish has no brain, but it can swim, catch food and even do something like sleeping. What does that make you wonder about brains?
items.a: It makes me wonder whether you need a brain to be alive and busy. Maybe nerves spread out through the body can do many of the jobs a brain does.
items.why: There is no single right answer. Jellyfish have a net of nerves through the body. One kind, the upside-down jellyfish, was found to have sleep-like rest at night.

items.p: If you could design an animal with no backbone that could live on land and be as big as a dog, how would it hold itself up and breathe? Explain your design.
items.a: Any well-reasoned answer. For example: it would have thick armour made of tubes, like a crab, with air holes all along its body and lungs inside. It would moult in a safe burrow.
items.why: Big land animals need a strong frame and a way to get oxygen deep inside. Good answers deal with both problems.

items.p: The octopus, a mollusc, and the fish, a vertebrate, both have eyes like cameras, with a lens. Their last shared ancestor had no such eyes. What does this tell us?
opts: Camera-like eyes appeared separately on two branches of the animal tree
All animals have the same eyes
items.why: Octopus eyes and our eyes grew from different starts, but ended up working in a similar way. Scientists call this convergent evolution. Picking 'octopuses are fish' mixes up looking alike with being related.

items.p: Draw a simple family tree with these animals on its branches: jellyfish, snail, ant, starfish, fish, you. Put the closest cousins next to each other.
items.a: Jellyfish on an early low branch. Then a split: snail and ant on one side, starfish, fish and you on the other side, with starfish branching off just before fish and you.
items.why: Jellyfish branched off early. Snails and insects share one big branch. Starfish share the other big branch with backboned animals.
items.art: A blank tree trunk with a few empty branches.

items.p: Why do scientists think there may be millions of kinds of animal still not discovered?
opts: Because animals are hiding on purpose
Because new insects, worms and sea animals are found every year, and places like the deep sea are hardly explored
Because old books lost the names
Because animals keep turning into new kinds every day
items.why: Every year scientists name thousands of new invertebrates. Huge places, like the deep sea floor and rainforest treetops, are barely explored. But nobody knows the exact number, so estimates differ a lot.

worksheets.context: This worksheet is for big thinkers: family trees, deep time, giant insects, open questions and designing your own animal.

experiments.title: Water Bones: how does a worm stay firm?
experiments.question: Does a long balloon get firmer the more water we squeeze into it?
experiments.predict: Before you test, look at three balloons: one with a little water, one half full and one full and tight. Guess which one will droop the least over the edge of a table.
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, use the same kind of balloon each time. Let the same length hang over the table edge, half the balloon. Measure the droop the same way, with a ruler held straight up and down. Test each balloon 3 times, because one try can be a fluke.

materials.item: long modelling balloons, all the same kind
water from a tap
a ruler
a table with a straight edge, and a tray or towel under it
a pencil and the results table

experiments.safety: Do this over a tray, outdoors or in the bathroom, because balloons can burst. Wipe up spills so nobody slips. Keep balloon pieces away from small children, who could choke on them.

schedule.what: Fill three balloons with different amounts of water. Measure how much each droops over a table edge. Squeeze the full one and measure how its length changes. Draw a bar chart.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw a bar chart with one bar for each balloon. A shorter bar means a firmer balloon.
experiments.context: This is the Water Bones experiment. You fill long balloons with different amounts of water and see how firm each one is. It shows how an earthworm stays firm with no bones.

setup.art: Three long balloons on a tray: one with a little water sagging at one end, one half full, one full and tight.
setup.caption: 1. Fill three balloons: a little water, half full, and full and tight.

setup.art: A full balloon laid on a table with half of it sticking out over the edge, and a ruler held straight up beside the end.
setup.caption: 2. Lay each balloon with half over the table edge.

setup.art: A ruler held upright from the table top down to the drooping tip of a balloon, the gap marked in centimetres.
setup.caption: 3. Measure how far the tip droops below the table top.

setup.art: Two hands squeezing the middle of the full balloon, which has grown longer than a ruler beside it.
setup.caption: 4. Squeeze the middle of the full balloon. Measure how long it gets.

example_chart.title: Made-up example: how far each balloon drooped over the table edge
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be different.

flow.do: 1. Fill one balloon with a little water, about a quarter. 2. Fill one about half. 3. Fill one as full and tight as you can. 4. Tie each one. Let out any air first.
flow.say: An earthworm has no bones. Today we will find out how it stays firm. Our balloons are pretend worms, full of different amounts of water.
flow.kid: Fill three long balloons with water: a little, half, and full and tight. A grown-up helps you tie them.
flow.parent: Long modelling balloons work best, but round balloons work too. Squeeze out the air before tying, so you are testing water only.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Water Bones experiment. You test how firm balloons are with different amounts of water inside, to see how a worm stays firm.

flow.do: Ask your child to guess which balloon will droop the least.
flow.say: Which balloon do you think will stay the straightest when half of it hangs over the edge? Why?
flow.kid: Which balloon will droop least? Guess. Why?

good: The full one has more water pushing out.

flow.do: 1. Lay a balloon on the table with half of it over the edge. 2. Hold the ruler straight up against the table edge. 3. Measure how far the tip hangs below the table top. 4. Write it in the table. 5. Do each balloon 3 times.
flow.say: Let's measure the droop. That is the gap from the table top down to the tip of the balloon. A small droop means a firm balloon.
flow.kid: Put half the balloon over the edge. Measure how far the tip hangs down. Write it down. Do each balloon 3 times.
flow.parent: To find the middle value, put the three numbers in order and take the middle one.

chart.title: Made-up example: how to fill in the table

flow.do: 1. Measure the length of the full balloon. 2. Squeeze its middle firmly all the way round with both hands. 3. Measure its length again.
flow.say: Now squeeze the middle of the full balloon. Watch the ends. This is what a worm's ring muscles do.
flow.kid: Measure the full balloon. Squeeze its middle with both hands. Measure it again. What happened?

check.q: When you squeeze the middle of a full water balloon, what happens?
check.why: Water cannot be squashed into less space. When you squeeze the middle, the water has to go somewhere, so it pushes the ends out and the balloon gets longer. A worm does the same with its ring muscles to push its front end forward. Picking 'shorter' is a natural guess, because squeezing usually makes things smaller.

flow.do: Help your child draw a bar chart of the middle droop values, one bar for each balloon.
flow.say: Let's turn our numbers into a picture. One bar for each balloon. Here a shorter bar means a firmer balloon.
flow.kid: Draw one bar for each balloon. A shorter bar means it drooped less. That one is firmest.

check.q: In the Water Bones bar chart, the full balloon has the shortest bar. What does that mean?
options: It drooped the least, so it was the firmest
check.why: The bar shows how far the tip drooped. The full, tight balloon drooped only a little, so it was the firmest. Picking 'floppiest' usually means thinking a short bar means 'less good'. Here a short bar means less droop.

chart.title: Made-up example: how far each balloon drooped over the table edge
chart.note: These numbers are made up. Your numbers will be different.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three sentences: what I think, what I saw, and why.
flow.say: Let's finish like scientists. What do you think now about how a worm stays firm? What did you see? Why?
flow.kid: Finish like a scientist. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer: What I think: a worm stays firm because it is full of liquid squeezed tight. What I saw: the full balloon drooped only 1 cm, but the one with a little water drooped 8 cm. Why: when water is packed in tight, it pushes out on every side, so the balloon can hold its shape without bones.

experiments.title: Armour Tubes: why are insect legs hollow tubes?
experiments.question: Which paper shape holds up the most weight: a round tube, a square tube or a zigzag?
experiments.predict: Before you test, make the three shapes from the same size paper. Guess which one will hold the most notebooks before it crumples.
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, use the same size and kind of paper for every shape, and the same amount of tape. Stand each shape on its end. Add notebooks of the same kind gently, one at a time, from the same height. Test each shape twice, with new paper each time.

materials.item: sheets of A4 paper, all the same kind
sticky tape
thin notebooks of the same size, or small paperback books
a ruler
the results table and a pencil

experiments.safety: Add notebooks gently and keep your face away from the top of the stack.

schedule.what: Make a round tube, a square tube and a zigzag from paper. Stand each one up and add notebooks until it crumples. Draw a bar chart.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw one bar for each shape, as tall as the number of notebooks it held.
experiments.context: This is the Armour Tubes experiment. You make paper pillars in three shapes and see which holds the most weight. It shows why the legs of insects, spiders and crabs are hollow tubes of armour.

setup.art: Three paper shapes standing on a table: a round tube, a square tube and a zigzag folded sheet, each taped.
setup.caption: 1. Make a round tube, a square tube and a zigzag from the same paper.

setup.art: A round paper tube standing on its end with a thin notebook resting flat on top.
setup.caption: 2. Stand one shape up. Put a notebook gently on top.

setup.art: A stack of notebooks on a crumpled paper tube, with a hand writing a number on a chart.
setup.caption: 3. Add notebooks one at a time until it crumples. Write down how many.

example_chart.title: Made-up example: how many notebooks each paper shape held
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be different.

flow.do: 1. Roll one sheet into a round tube along its long side and tape it. 2. Fold one sheet into four long strips and tape it into a square tube. 3. Fold one sheet back and forth into a zigzag fan.
flow.say: Insects, spiders and crabs wear their skeleton on the outside, as armour. Their legs are hollow tubes. Let's find out why tubes are a good idea.
flow.kid: Make three shapes from paper: a round tube, a square tube and a zigzag. Tape them.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Armour Tubes experiment. You test which paper shape is strongest, to see why armoured legs are tubes.

flow.do: Ask your child to guess which shape will hold the most.
flow.say: Which one do you think will hold the most notebooks before it crumples? Why?
flow.kid: Which shape will hold the most? Guess. Why?

good: The round one has no weak corners.
The zigzag has lots of folds.
The tube is like a pipe.

flow.do: 1. Stand a shape on its end. 2. Lay a notebook gently on top, flat. 3. Keep adding notebooks one at a time until the shape bends or crumples. 4. Write down how many it held before it crumpled. 5. Test each shape twice, with fresh paper.
flow.say: Gently now. One notebook at a time. Stop when it crumples, and count how many it held.
flow.kid: Stand a shape up. Add notebooks one at a time. When it crumples, count how many it held.
flow.parent: Lower each notebook gently. Dropping it is not fair, because a falling notebook pushes harder.

chart.title: Made-up example: how to fill in the table

flow.do: Help your child draw a bar chart, one bar for each shape.
flow.say: Let's draw one bar for each shape. A taller bar means a stronger shape.
flow.kid: Draw one bar for each shape. A taller bar means it held more.

check.q: In the Armour Tubes chart, which shape is strongest?
options: The zigzag, because it has the most folds
The round tube, because its bar is tallest
The square tube, because it has corners
check.why: The round tube held the most notebooks, so its bar is tallest. The weight spreads evenly all the way round a tube. Picking the zigzag is a good guess, because folds do make paper stiffer, but a zigzag can fall sideways.

chart.title: Made-up example: how many notebooks each paper shape held
chart.note: These numbers are made up. Your numbers will be different.

flow.do: Ask your child to say three sentences: what I think, what I saw, and why.
flow.say: Let's finish like scientists. Why do you think an ant's legs are hollow tubes of armour? What did you see? Why?
flow.kid: Finish like a scientist. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer: What I think: tubes are a strong shape for armour. What I saw: the round tube held 7 notebooks, but the zigzag held only 2. Why: a tube spreads the weight all the way round, and it is hollow, so it is strong without being heavy. Your own long bones are hollow tubes too.
flow.think: Bicycle frames, bamboo and the bones in your legs are all tubes. Why do you think so many strong things are tubes?

experiments.title: Many Small Suckers: how does a starfish hold on?
experiments.question: Do more small suckers hold more weight?
experiments.predict: Before you test, guess how many cups of rice one sucker can hold. Then guess for two suckers and four suckers.
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, use the same kind of sucker each time, on the same clean, smooth tile. Press each sucker on in the same way. Add rice one cup at a time, gently. Test each number of suckers twice.

materials.item: small rubber suction cups with hooks, all the same size
a smooth tiled wall or a large smooth tile
a cloth bag with handles
string
uncooked rice and a small cup to measure it
a towel on the floor underneath

experiments.safety: Put a towel underneath, because the bag will drop. Keep your feet out of the way. Hang it low, about knee height.

schedule.what: Hang a bag from 1, 2 and then 4 suckers on a tile. Add rice until the suckers pop off. Draw a bar chart.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw one bar for each number of suckers.
experiments.context: This is the Many Small Suckers experiment. You hang a bag of rice from rubber suckers on a tile to see how many small grips add up. It shows how a starfish holds on with hundreds of tube feet.

setup.art: One small rubber suction cup with a hook pressed onto a clean bathroom wall tile at knee height, a towel on the floor below.
setup.caption: 1. Press one sucker onto a smooth tile, low down.

setup.art: A cloth bag hanging from the sucker's hook by a short string, a cup of rice being poured in.
setup.caption: 2. Hang a bag. Add rice one cup at a time.

setup.art: Four suckers in a row on the tile, each tied by string to the same cloth bag, holding a heavier load.
setup.caption: 3. Try again with two suckers, then four, all tied to the same bag.

example_chart.title: Made-up example: cups of rice held before the suckers popped off
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be different.

flow.do: 1. Wipe a smooth tile clean and dry. 2. Wet each sucker a little. 3. Press one sucker firmly onto the tile at about knee height. 4. Spread a towel underneath.
flow.say: A starfish has hundreds of tiny tube feet under its arms. Each one grips like a little sucker. Let's find out what happens when many small grips work together.
flow.kid: Clean a tile. Wet a sucker a little. Press it hard on the tile, low down. Put a towel underneath.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Many Small Suckers experiment. You find out how many small suckers can hold more than one, like a starfish's tube feet.

flow.do: Ask your child to guess how many cups of rice one sucker will hold, and then two and four.
flow.say: How many cups do you think one sucker will hold? What about two? Four?
flow.kid: Guess. How many cups will one sucker hold? Two suckers? Four?

flow.do: 1. Hang the bag from the sucker with a short string. 2. Pour in rice one cup at a time, gently. 3. When the sucker pops off, write how many full cups it held. 4. Now use two suckers, each tied to the bag. 5. Then four. 6. Test each twice.
flow.say: One cup at a time, gently. When it pops, we write down the last number of cups it held.
flow.kid: Add rice one cup at a time. When the sucker pops off, write how many cups it held. Then try two suckers, then four.
flow.parent: Tie each sucker's hook to the bag handle with its own short string, so they share the load. Pour the rice back into its tin afterwards to use again.

chart.title: Made-up example: how to fill in the table

flow.do: Help your child draw a bar chart, one bar for each number of suckers.
flow.say: Let's draw the bars. What happens to the bars as we add suckers?
flow.kid: Draw one bar for each number of suckers. Do the bars grow?

check.q: In the Many Small Suckers chart, 4 suckers held about 4 times as much as 1 sucker. What does that tell us about a starfish?
options: One big tube foot would be better
Hundreds of small tube feet together can grip very strongly
Starfish do not need to grip
check.why: Each tube foot is weak by itself, but hundreds of them pulling together make a strong grip. That is how a starfish can pull open a clam shell. Picking 'one big tube foot' is a fair idea, but many small grips also let a starfish hold on to bumpy rocks, where one big sucker would not fit.

chart.title: Made-up example: cups of rice held before the suckers popped off
chart.note: These numbers are made up. Your numbers will be different.

flow.do: Ask your child to say three sentences: what I think, what I saw, and why.
flow.say: Let's finish like scientists. What do you think? What did you see? Why?
flow.kid: Finish like a scientist. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer: What I think: more suckers hold more weight. What I saw: one sucker held 3 cups and four suckers held 11 cups. Why: each sucker grips a little, and their grips add up. A starfish has hundreds of tube feet, so it holds on very tightly.
flow.think: Four suckers held 11 cups, not exactly 12. Why might they not add up perfectly?

activities.title: Backbone Census: who lives in one small patch?

materials.item: a magnifying glass, if you have one
a paper and pencil for tally marks
4 sticks or pencils and a piece of string, to mark a square about as wide as your arms
a white plate or sheet of paper, for looking at small animals

activities.safety: Go outdoors only with a grown-up. Do not touch spiders, scorpions, centipedes or caterpillars with hairs. Lift stones with a stick, away from you, and put them back gently. Wash your hands with soap afterwards.

schedule.what: Feel your backbone. Mark a small patch outdoors. Look for 10 minutes and tally animals with and without a backbone. Draw a bar chart and say what you found.

activities.record: Make two tally columns: BACKBONE and NO BACKBONE. Add a tally mark for each kind of animal you see. Then draw two bars.
activities.context: This is a count of the animals in one small patch outdoors. You sort them into animals with a backbone and without one, to see which kind there are more of.

setup.art: A child bending forward while a parent's finger traces the bumps of her backbone.
setup.caption: 1. Feel your backbone first.

setup.art: A square of string tied to four sticks on a patch of grass and soil beside a garden wall, with a flowerpot and a stone inside it.
setup.caption: 2. Mark a small square outdoors with sticks and string.

setup.art: A child crouched over the square with a magnifying glass, looking at ants, a worm and a woodlouse, while a sparrow hops near the edge.
setup.caption: 3. Look closely for 10 minutes. Look low and high.

setup.art: A sheet with two tally columns, a few marks under a bird symbol and many marks under an ant symbol.
setup.caption: 4. Make a tally mark for each kind of animal.

example_chart.title: Made-up example: kinds of animal found in one patch in 10 minutes
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be different.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to bend forward. 2. Run a finger gently down the middle of their back, from the neck to the bottom.
flow.say: Can you feel these bumps? This is your backbone. It is a chain of small bones that holds you up. Today we will find out how many animals around us have one.
flow.kid: Bend forward. Ask a grown-up to run a finger down your back. Feel the bumps? That is your backbone.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Backbone Census. You count the animals in one small patch, and sort them by whether they have a backbone.

flow.do: Before going out, ask your child to guess.
flow.say: Do you think we will find more animals with a backbone, or more without one? Make a guess, and say why.
flow.kid: Guess first. Will you find more animals with a backbone, or without one? Why?

good: I see lots of birds and dogs.
There are lots of ants everywhere.
Small animals hide, so maybe more of them.

flow.parent: Most children guess backbone animals, because birds, dogs and cats are the animals they notice. That is a great guess to test.

flow.do: 1. Go outdoors together. 2. Choose a patch with some soil, plants, a stone or a flowerpot. 3. Push the four sticks in to make a square about as wide as your child's arms, and tie the string around them.
flow.say: Let's mark our patch. We will only count animals inside this square, or flying just over it.
flow.kid: Go outside with a grown-up. Make a square with sticks and string. Only count animals in your square.
flow.parent: A balcony pot or a corner of a park is fine. If you cannot go out, use one room: a kitchen window, the sink area and a corner of the floor.

flow.do: 1. Look closely for 10 minutes. 2. Look on leaves, under leaves, on the soil, and under a stone or pot lifted with a stick. 3. For each new kind of animal, make one tally mark in the right column. 4. Put stones back exactly as they were.
flow.say: Look high and low. Under leaves. In the cracks. Under that stone, which I'll lift with a stick. Every new kind of animal gets one tally mark.
flow.kid: Look closely. Under leaves. In cracks. Under a stone a grown-up lifts. One tally mark for each new kind of animal.
flow.parent: Count kinds, not individuals. Twenty ants of the same kind count as one mark. Two different ants, a big black one and a tiny red one, count as two. Common finds: ants, woodlice, earthworms, spiders, snails, slugs, beetles, flies, mosquitoes, millipedes, springtails. Backbone animals you may see: a sparrow, a myna, a gecko, a frog, a squirrel.

check.q: You find 30 small black ants, all the same kind. How many tally marks do they get?
options: No marks, ants are too small
check.why: We are counting kinds of animal, not single animals. All 30 ants are one kind, so they get one mark. Picking 30 is counting every ant, which is a different question. It is a good one too, but it is not this count.

flow.do: Count the tally marks in each column. Then draw two bars side by side, one for each group.
flow.say: Let's count our marks. Now let's draw one bar for backbone animals, and one for animals without a backbone.
flow.kid: Count your marks. Draw two bars. Make each bar as tall as its number.

chart.title: Made-up example: kinds of animal found in one patch in 10 minutes
chart.note: These numbers are made up. Your numbers will be different.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Let's finish like real scientists. What do you think now? What did you see? And why do you think there were so many of one kind?
flow.kid: Finish like a scientist. Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: there are more animals without a backbone. What I saw: we found 11 kinds without a backbone and only 2 with one. Why: small animals can live in tiny places like under a stone or on one leaf, and there are lots of those places.

check.q: In the census, you found 11 kinds of animal without a backbone and 2 kinds with one. What does this show?
options: Animals with a backbone do not live here
In our patch, there were many more kinds of animal without a backbone
Small animals are not real animals
check.why: The count shows more kinds of invertebrate in your patch, just as scientists find all over the world. Picking 'do not live here' goes too far: you did find 2 kinds. Picking 'not real animals' is a common habit. Ants and worms are animals as much as cows are.

activities.title: Leg Count Key: insect, spider, crab or centipede?

materials.item: the 12 minibeast cards from Guess My Minibeast, or real minibeasts seen in a clear box
a magnifying glass
a pencil and paper

activities.safety: If you catch a real minibeast to look at, use a clear box and a paintbrush, never your fingers. Look for 5 minutes, then let it go where you found it. Do not catch spiders, scorpions or centipedes.

schedule.what: Use the leg count key to name 6 minibeasts, then make your own key question.

activities.record: For each animal, write the questions you answered and the group you reached.
activities.context: This is a key, a set of yes or no questions that leads you to an animal's group. You use it to tell insects, spiders, crabs and centipedes apart by counting legs.

setup.caption: 1. Look closely at one animal. Count its legs.

setup.art: A simple flow chart drawn on paper with yes and no arrows: Legs? 6? 8? 10? Many?
setup.caption: 2. Follow the questions on the key.

setup.art: A child writing 'insect' beside a drawing of an ant, and 'arachnid' beside a spider.
setup.caption: 3. Write the group you reached.

flow.do: Write this key on paper. 1: Does it have legs? No: worm or snail. Yes: go to 2. 2: Does it have exactly 6 legs? Yes: insect. No: go to 3. 3: Does it have exactly 8 legs? Yes: arachnid, like a spider. No: go to 4. 4: Does it have 10 legs? Yes: crab or prawn. No: go to 5. 5: Does it have lots of legs on a long ringed body? Yes: centipede or millipede.
flow.say: This is a key. It is a list of yes or no questions. Each answer sends you to the next question, until you reach the animal's group.
flow.kid: This is a key. Answer each question yes or no. Follow the arrows to the animal's group.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Leg Count Key. You use yes or no questions about legs to find the group a small animal belongs to.

flow.do: Take the cards one by one. Your child counts the legs and follows the key out loud.
flow.say: Let's try the ant. Does it have legs? Yes. Exactly 6? Yes. So the ant is an insect.
flow.kid: Pick a card. Count the legs. Follow the key. Which group is it?

check.q: A woodlouse has 14 legs. It is not long and thin like a centipede. Where does the key leave it?
options: The key does not have a place for it, so we need a new question
check.why: The key only knows 0, 6, 8, 10 or lots of legs on a long body. A woodlouse has 14 legs and a short, rounded body, so the key gets stuck. That is not a mistake. It means we need a new question. Woodlice are land cousins of crabs and prawns. Picking 'insect' is the most common guess, because woodlice are small and live on land.

flow.do: Look at the ant and the spider cards side by side. Count their body parts.
flow.say: Count the body parts too. The ant has a head, a middle and a back end. How many parts does the spider have? And does it have feelers?
flow.kid: Look at the ant and the spider. Count their body parts. Which one has feelers?

ask.q: What two things show a spider is not an insect?

flow.do: Ask your child to add one new question to the key, so the woodlouse has a place.
flow.say: Can you add one question that would find the woodlouse? Scientists improve their keys like this all the time.
flow.kid: Add one new question to the key. Make it find the woodlouse.
flow.parent: Any question that works is good. For example: 'Does it have 14 legs and roll into a ball?' or 'Does it have a short body and more than 10 legs?'
flow.think: Would your key work for an animal from the sea, like a starfish? What question would you add for it?

activities.title: Snail Foot Window: watch a snail walk from underneath

materials.item: a garden snail, found after rain on a wall or plant
a clear glass sheet, a clear plastic box lid or a clean glass tumbler laid on its side
a few drops of water
a magnifying glass

activities.safety: Wash your hands well with soap and water after touching a snail or its slime. Some snails can carry germs. Never put a snail near your mouth. If you find a large snail with a long cone-shaped shell, that may be the giant African snail. Look, but do not touch it.

schedule.what: Put a snail on clear plastic or glass. Watch the waves under its foot. Draw what you see. Put it back.

activities.record: Draw the snail's foot from underneath, with the waves. Write how many waves you counted at one time.
activities.context: In this activity you watch a garden snail from underneath, through clear glass or plastic. You see the waves of muscle that move its one big foot.

setup.art: A grown-up's hand gently lifting a garden snail off a wet wall after rain.
setup.caption: 1. After rain, find a snail on a wall or plant.

setup.art: A snail on a clear plastic lid with a few drops of water on it, held up by two stacks of books.
setup.caption: 2. Put it on clear plastic with a few drops of water.

setup.art: A child lying on the floor looking up through the plastic at the underside of the snail's foot, with dark stripes running across it.
setup.caption: 3. Look from underneath at the stripes on its foot.

flow.do: 1. After rain, find a garden snail on a wall or plant. 2. Lift it gently by the shell, not the soft body. 3. Wet a clear plastic lid with a few drops of water.
flow.say: A snail has no bones and no legs. It walks on one big soft foot. Let's watch that foot from underneath.
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to help you find a snail after rain. Hold it gently by the shell.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Snail Foot Window. You watch a snail walk on clear plastic and look at its foot from below.

flow.do: Put the snail on the wet plastic. Rest the plastic on two stacks of books, so you can look up at it from underneath. Wait until the snail comes out and starts moving.
flow.say: We have to be patient. A snail comes out when it feels safe.
flow.kid: Put the snail on the wet plastic. Wait quietly until it comes out and moves.
flow.parent: If it stays inside its shell, put one drop of water on it and wait a few minutes in the shade.

flow.do: Look up from underneath. Watch the dark stripes moving along the foot. Count how many stripes you can see at one time.
flow.say: Look at the dark stripes moving along its foot. Each stripe is a wave of muscle squeezing. The snail rides on these waves and on its slime.
flow.kid: Look from underneath. See the dark stripes moving? Count them. Each one is a squeeze of muscle.

options: Waves of muscle along its one foot, sliding on slime
Its shell rolls like a wheel
check.why: A snail has no legs and no bones. Waves of muscle ripple along its foot, and its slime helps it grip and glide. Picking 'tiny legs' is a common guess, because most crawling things we know have legs. Look again from underneath: you will see stripes, not legs.

flow.do: Look at the shiny trail it leaves. Then put the snail back exactly where you found it.
flow.say: See the shiny trail? That is its slime. Let's take it home now, where we found it.
flow.kid: Look at the shiny slime trail. Then help put the snail back where you found it. Wash your hands with soap.

flow.do: Ask your child to draw the foot from underneath and say three things: what I think, what I saw and why.
flow.say: Draw what you saw. Then tell me: what do you think moves a snail? What did you see? Why does that make sense?
flow.kid: Draw the foot from underneath. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer: What I think: a snail moves by squeezing its foot. What I saw: dark stripes moved along the foot from back to front. Why: each stripe is a squeeze, and the squeezes push the snail along on its slime.

activities.title: Jellyfish in a Bottle

materials.item: a clear plastic bottle with a lid, about 1 litre
a thin plastic bag, like a vegetable bag
a thread or thin rubber band
scissors
water, with 1 or 2 drops of blue food colour if you like

activities.safety: A grown-up does the cutting. Wipe up any spilled water so nobody slips.

schedule.what: Make a plastic bag jellyfish. Watch it float in water, then lift it out and watch it flop.

activities.record: Draw your jellyfish in the bottle and out of the bottle. Write why it changes shape.
activities.context: In this activity you make a model jellyfish from a plastic bag. You see how a body with no bones keeps its shape in water, and flops out of water.

setup.art: A flat plastic bag with a small puffed bubble tied off at the top with thread, and the rest cut into long thin strips.
setup.caption: 1. Tie a small bubble at the top of a bag. Cut the rest into strips.

setup.art: A clear bottle full of water with the plastic jellyfish floating inside, its strips spread like tentacles.
setup.caption: 2. Put it in a bottle of water and close the lid.

setup.art: A hand lifting the dripping plastic jellyfish out of the water, all its strips stuck together in a limp clump.
setup.caption: 3. Lift it out. Watch it flop.

flow.do: 1. Lay a thin plastic bag flat. 2. Pinch the middle of the closed end to make a small air bubble about the size of a lime. 3. Tie it off with thread. 4. A grown-up cuts the rest of the bag into 8 long, thin strips.
flow.say: A jellyfish has no bones, no brain and no heart. It is about 95 parts in every 100 water. Let's make one and see how it stays in shape.
flow.kid: Pinch a small bubble at the top of a plastic bag. Tie it. A grown-up cuts the rest into thin strips. These are tentacles.
flow.context: This is the first step of Jellyfish in a Bottle. You make a model jellyfish from a plastic bag.

flow.do: Fill the bottle almost to the top with water. Push the jellyfish in, add water to the very top and close the lid. Turn the bottle slowly.
flow.say: Watch the tentacles spread out. The water holds them up, the way the sea holds up a real jellyfish.
flow.kid: Put the jellyfish in the bottle of water. Close the lid. Turn the bottle slowly. Watch it float.

ask.q: What holds the jellyfish's shape in the water?
good: The water holds the tentacles apart.

flow.do: Take the jellyfish out and hold it up by the bubble.
flow.say: Now look. What happened to its shape?
flow.kid: Take it out. Hold it up. What happens to its tentacles?

check.q: Out of the water, the plastic jellyfish flops into a clump. What does that tell us about real jellyfish?
options: Real jellyfish have bones that break in air
Jellyfish have no skeleton, so the water holds their shape
check.why: A jellyfish has no bones and no armour. The sea holds it up. On a beach, it collapses into a blob. Picking 'bones that break' mixes jellyfish up with fish. Jellyfish have no bones at all.

flow.do: Ask your child to draw the jellyfish in and out of water, and say three things: what I think, what I saw and why.
flow.say: Draw both pictures. Then tell me what you think, what you saw, and why.
flow.kid: Draw it in the water and out of it. Say what you think, what you saw and why.
flow.parent: A good answer: What I think: jellyfish need water to hold their shape. What I saw: in the bottle the strips spread out, but in the air they stuck together in a clump. Why: the jellyfish has no skeleton, and the water was holding it up.
flow.think: Why might a real jellyfish washed up on a beach still sting you, even if it looks like a flat blob?

activities.title: Grow Out of Your Armour: act out a moult

materials.item: a sheet of old newspaper or chart paper
sticky tape
a small folded towel or a pair of socks

activities.safety: Keep the tape off skin and hair. Make the paper tube loose enough to slide.

schedule.what: Wear a paper armour tube on your arm, grow inside it, split it and climb out.

activities.record: Draw the three stages: armour on, armour split, new armour.
activities.context: This is an act-it-out activity. You wear a paper tube on your arm like a crab's armour, then 'grow' until it splits, to feel why armoured animals must moult.

setup.art: A paper tube taped around a child's forearm like a sleeve of armour.
setup.caption: 1. Tape a paper tube around your arm, a little loose.

setup.art: A grown-up sliding a folded towel inside the tube, which is bulging and starting to tear.
setup.caption: 2. Grow: push a folded towel inside the tube.

setup.art: A child pulling a bigger arm out of the split paper tube, with a new, larger paper tube waiting on the table.
setup.caption: 3. Split the old armour, climb out, and put on a bigger one.

flow.do: Roll the paper around your child's forearm, a little loose, and tape it into a tube.
flow.say: This tube is your armour, like a crab's shell. It is hard on the outside, and you are soft inside.
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to tape a paper tube around your arm. This is your armour.
flow.context: This is the first step of Grow Out of Your Armour. You wear paper armour and find out why animals with armour must moult.

flow.do: Now your child 'grows'. Slowly push a folded towel or socks inside the tube, next to the arm.
flow.say: You are growing. Your body gets bigger. But the armour cannot stretch. What happens?
flow.kid: Now you grow. A towel goes inside the tube. Feel it get tight.

ask.q: How does it feel when you grow inside the armour?

flow.do: Let the tube split along the tape. Your child slides out. Make a new, bigger tube from fresh paper, but leave it untaped for one minute, as 'soft armour'.
flow.say: The old armour splits and you climb out. For a while your new armour is soft. A real crab hides at this time, because it is easy to eat.
flow.kid: Split the tube. Climb out. Your new armour is soft for a while. Hide!

check.q: Why does a crab hide after it moults?
options: It is tired of its friends
Its new armour is still soft, so it is easy to hurt
Crabs only come out at night
check.why: After a moult, the new shell takes some days to harden. Until then the crab is soft and easy for hunters to catch. Picking 'lost its legs' is a mix-up: a crab keeps its legs when it moults. It pulls them out of the old shell like fingers from a glove.

flow.do: Ask your child to draw the three stages and say why armour and growing are a problem.
flow.say: Draw the three pictures. Why can't armour just grow with the animal, like your bones grow with you?
flow.kid: Draw armour on, armour split and new armour. Why can't armour stretch?
flow.parent: Bones are alive and grow from inside, with blood in them. An exoskeleton is a hard outer layer that cannot grow, so it must be replaced.

activities.title: Spider Web Morning

materials.item: a spray bottle with water, set to a fine mist
a torch, if it is early and dim
paper and a dark pencil

activities.safety: Never touch a spider. Keep your hands away from the web. Spray from at least an arm's length away, and only a light mist. Go out with a grown-up.

schedule.what: Find a web early in the morning. Mist it gently. Count the spokes and draw it.

activities.record: Draw the web. Write how many spokes it has, and where the spider was waiting.
activities.context: In this activity you find a spider's web early in the morning. You mist it gently so the silk shows up, then count its spokes and draw it.

setup.art: A round spider web between two branches of a hibiscus bush, sparkling with dew in early morning light.
setup.caption: 1. Find a web early in the morning, between plants.

setup.art: A child holding a spray bottle an arm's length away from the web, a fine mist drifting onto it.
setup.caption: 2. Mist it gently from an arm's length away.

setup.art: A drawing of a round web with its spokes numbered from 1 to 20 around the edge.
setup.caption: 3. Count the spokes and draw the web.

flow.do: Go out early with your child. Look between plants, along railings and in window corners for a round web.
flow.say: Spiders are not insects. They have 8 legs. Many spiders spin silk webs to catch insects. Webs are easiest to see in the early morning.
flow.kid: Go out with a grown-up early in the morning. Look for a round spider web.
flow.context: This is the first step of Spider Web Morning. You find a spider's web and look closely at how it is built.

flow.do: Spray a light mist onto the web from at least an arm's length away.
flow.say: Watch the silk appear. Each drop of water hangs on a thread like a bead.
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to spray a light mist on the web. Watch the threads sparkle.

flow.do: Count the spokes running out from the middle. Look for the spiral thread. Look for the spider, often in the middle or hiding at the edge.
flow.say: Count the spokes, the straight threads from the middle. Then look for the round spiral. Where is the spider waiting?
flow.kid: Count the straight spokes. Look for the spiral. Can you see the spider? Do not touch it.

check.q: A spider has 8 legs, 2 body parts and no feelers. Which group is it in?
check.why: Spiders are arachnids, with scorpions and mites. Picking 'insects' is the most common mix-up, because spiders catch insects and live in the same places. But insects have 6 legs and 3 body parts.

flow.do: Ask your child to draw the web and write how many spokes it had.
flow.say: Draw the web. A spider spins all of that from silk made inside its own body. Spider silk is one of the toughest threads known.
flow.kid: Draw the web. Write how many spokes it had.
flow.parent: Common round-web spiders in Indian gardens include the giant wood spider and the signature spider, which makes a zigzag pattern in its web. Most garden spiders are harmless to people but should never be handled.
flow.think: The spider made all this silk inside its own small body. Where do you think the stuff for the silk comes from?

activities.title: Five-Arm Fold: the starfish shape

materials.item: a square of paper
scissors
a pencil

activities.safety: A grown-up helps with the scissors.

schedule.what: Fold and cut a five-armed star. Compare its symmetry with your own body.

activities.record: Draw a line down your own picture where the two halves match. Draw lines on the star where its parts match.
activities.context: In this activity you cut a five-armed star from folded paper. You compare a starfish's five matching parts with your own two matching sides.

setup.art: A square of paper folded into a thin wedge, like a slice of cake, with a pencil line drawn across it.
setup.caption: 1. Fold the paper into five equal parts, like a slice of cake.

setup.art: Scissors cutting along the pencil line on the folded paper wedge.
setup.caption: 2. Cut along the line.

setup.art: An opened five-armed paper star next to a child's outline with one mirror line down the middle.
setup.caption: 3. Open it. Compare the star with your own body.

flow.do: Fold a square of paper in half to make a triangle. Then fold it into five equal parts, like a fan. A grown-up cuts a slanted line across the folded wedge.
flow.say: A starfish has five arms, all the same, around a middle. Let's make one by folding.
flow.kid: Fold the paper into five parts, like a fan. A grown-up helps you cut across it.
flow.parent: An exact five-way fold is tricky. Fold into a triangle, then fold the triangle into a fan of five roughly equal parts. If it comes out with four or six points, that is fine. Talk about it.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Five-Arm Fold. You make a paper star to see how a starfish's body is built in five matching parts.

flow.do: Open the star. Turn it slowly on the table.
flow.say: Turn it slowly. Every time you turn it a little, it looks the same. Now look at your own body. Where are your matching parts?
flow.kid: Open your star. Turn it. It looks the same each time. Now look at yourself. Where do you match?

check.q: How is a starfish's body built differently from yours?
options: It has a left side and a right side, like us
It has five matching parts around a middle
It has a backbone in each arm
check.why: You have one line down the middle: your left side matches your right. A starfish has five matching parts around a centre, like the spokes of a wheel. Picking 'backbone in each arm' is a guess many children make because the arms look stiff. But a starfish has no bones, only hard chalky plates under its skin.

flow.do: Talk about regrowing. Fold one arm of the paper star back under.
flow.say: If a starfish loses an arm, it can grow a new one over many months. Some starfish can even grow a new body from one arm, if part of the middle comes with it.
flow.kid: Fold one arm under. A real starfish could grow it back. It takes months.
flow.think: Your skin can mend a cut. Your hair grows back. Can you grow back a finger? Why do you think some animals can and some cannot?

projects.title: Bottle Wormery: watch worms mix the soil

materials.item: a large clear plastic bottle, about 2 litres, with the top cut off by a grown-up
garden soil, dark and damp
sand, pale coloured
a handful of dead leaves and some vegetable peels
3 to 5 earthworms, found after rain or in damp soil
a dark cloth or black paper to wrap round the bottle
a spray bottle with water

projects.safety: A grown-up cuts the bottle. Handle worms gently with wet hands, and only for a moment. Wash your hands with soap after touching soil or worms. Keep the wormery out of the sun. After 14 days, return the worms to where you found them.

schedule.what: Build the wormery in layers of soil and sand. Add leaves and peels. Add the worms. Wrap it in dark cloth. Draw the layers.
Unwrap and look. Are the layers still sharp? Draw what you see. Mist the top if it is dry.
Look again. Are any leaves pulled down? Are there tunnels against the glass? Draw it.
Look and draw. Mist the soil if it is dry.
Draw the final layers. Compare all your drawings. Return the worms to the soil where you found them.

projects.record: On each day, draw the bottle and its layers in the same way. At the end, put your drawings in a row and write what the worms did.
projects.context: In this 14-day project you make a see-through home for earthworms, with layers of soil and sand. You watch how the worms mix the layers and pull leaves underground.

setup.art: A tall cut-off plastic bottle with neat stripes of dark soil and pale sand, leaves on top, and a few earthworms on the surface.
setup.caption: 1. Fill a bottle with layers of damp soil and sand. Put leaves and worms on top.

setup.art: The same bottle wrapped in a dark cloth, standing in a shady corner of a room.
setup.caption: 2. Wrap it in dark cloth. Worms like the dark.

setup.art: The bottle unwrapped after two weeks, the stripes blurred and mixed, tunnels visible against the plastic and leaves pulled down.
setup.caption: 3. After two weeks, the layers are mixed and leaves are pulled down.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up cuts the top off a large bottle. 2. Your child fills it with layers: 4 cm of damp soil, then 2 cm of sand, then soil, then sand, to near the top. 3. Mist each layer so it is damp, not wet. 4. Put dead leaves and peels on top.
flow.say: Charles Darwin, a famous scientist, spent about 40 years studying earthworms. He thought they were some of the most important animals in the world. Let's find out why.
flow.kid: Make stripes in the bottle: soil, then sand, then soil, then sand. Keep them damp. Put leaves on top.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Bottle Wormery, a 14-day project. You build a striped bottle of soil and sand and add earthworms, to watch what they do.

flow.do: 1. Find 3 to 5 earthworms in damp soil, or on the ground after rain. 2. Wet your hands. 3. Put the worms gently on top of the leaves. 4. Wrap the bottle in dark cloth and put it in a cool, shady place.
flow.say: Worms breathe through their damp skin, so we keep everything damp. They do not like light, so we wrap the bottle in dark cloth.
flow.kid: Find a few worms with a grown-up. Wet your hands. Put the worms gently on top. Wrap the bottle in dark cloth.

flow.do: Draw the bottle with its stripes, carefully, on day 1.
flow.say: Let's draw it now, so we can compare. Draw every stripe exactly as it is.
flow.kid: Draw your bottle. Draw each stripe clearly. You will compare later.

ask.q: What do you think the worms will do to the stripes?

flow.do: On day 3, 7 and 10, unwrap the bottle, look closely, and draw it again. Mist the top if it is dry.
flow.say: Look closely against the plastic. Can you see tunnels? Are the stripes still sharp? Are any leaves pulled down?
flow.kid: Unwrap the bottle. Look for tunnels and mixed stripes. Draw it. Mist it if it is dry.
flow.wait: Come back on day 3, day 7 and day 10.

check.q: After a week in the wormery, the stripes of soil and sand are blurred and mixed. Who mixed them?
options: The earthworms, moving up and down through the soil
Nobody, the stripes faded by themselves
check.why: Earthworms tunnel up and down. They swallow soil at one level and leave it at another, and they pull leaves down from the top. Picking 'the water' is a fair idea to test. You could make a second bottle with no worms and compare.

flow.do: On day 14, draw the bottle one last time. Lay all the drawings in a row. Then return the worms to the soil where you found them.
flow.say: Put your drawings in a row, from day 1 to day 14. What changed? Tell me three things: what you think, what you saw, and why.
flow.kid: Put your drawings in a row. What changed? Say what you think, what you saw and why. Then put the worms back in the soil.
flow.parent: A good answer: What I think: worms mix the soil. What I saw: on day 1 the stripes were sharp, and by day 14 they were blurred, with tunnels and leaves pulled down. Why: worms tunnel and eat soil and leaves, carrying them up and down. This lets air and water into the soil and feeds plants.

challenges.title: Armour That Can Grow
challenges.problem: Crabs and insects must split their armour to grow, and then they are soft and in danger for a while. Design a suit of armour for a toy, or for your own arm, that can get bigger without being thrown away.
constraints: The armour must cover the whole arm or toy, with no big gaps.
It must still let the arm bend at the elbow.
It must be able to get at least 2 cm wider around without breaking.
Use only paper, card, tape, string and things from home.
materials: a measuring tape or a string and ruler
general: Make overlapping plates, like roof tiles or a woodlouse's back. As the arm grows, the plates slide apart but still overlap.
Make the armour in rings with gaps between them, like the segments of an earthworm or a prawn's tail.
Add a seam with a lace, like a shoe. Loosen the lace as the arm grows.
creative: A hermit crab does not grow armour at all. It borrows empty snail shells and moves into a bigger one when it grows. Could your toy swap armour with a friend?
Snails solve the problem by adding new shell at the open edge. Could you add a new strip at the end of your armour each week?
Real armadillos and pangolins have backbones, but they use overlapping scales. Look at pictures of a pangolin for ideas.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own armour that can grow. Draw it, build it, and test it by slipping a folded cloth under it to 'grow' 2 cm. Does it still cover everything? Does the elbow still bend?
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. Animals with armour must moult to grow. Your job is to invent armour that can grow without being thrown away.

setup.art: A child's arm wrapped in overlapping card plates like roof tiles, held together with string.
setup.caption: 1. Build armour from overlapping plates or rings.

setup.art: A folded cloth being slid under the card armour, the plates sliding apart but still overlapping.
setup.caption: 2. Test it: slide a cloth under it to 'grow' 2 cm.

setup.art: The child bending the armoured elbow, with a measuring tape around the armour.
setup.caption: 3. Check that the elbow bends and nothing has a gap.

flow.do: Read the problem together. Look at pictures of a crab, a woodlouse and a prawn's tail.
flow.say: A crab's armour cannot grow, so it has to break out of it. Can we invent armour that grows with you?
flow.kid: Read the problem. Armour that can grow. Look at how a woodlouse's back is made of plates.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Armour That Can Grow challenge. You design armour that can get bigger without being thrown away.

flow.do: Ask your child to draw at least two ideas before building.
flow.say: Draw two ideas first. Engineers always draw before they build.
flow.kid: Draw two ideas for armour that can grow.

ask.q: How will your armour get bigger?
good: I add a new piece at the end.

flow.do: Build the best idea from card, paper, tape and string. A grown-up cuts the card.
flow.say: Let's build it. Remember: it must cover the arm, bend at the elbow and grow 2 cm.
flow.kid: Build your armour. A grown-up helps with cutting.

flow.do: Measure around the armour. Slide a folded cloth underneath to make the arm 'grow'. Measure again. Check the elbow bends and look for gaps.
flow.say: Let's test it. Measure around. Now grow. Measure again. Any gaps? Does the elbow bend?
flow.kid: Measure around your armour. Slide a cloth under it. Measure again. Any gaps?

check.q: Why do overlapping plates let armour grow?
options: The plates get bigger by themselves
The plates can slide apart and still cover the gap
check.why: When the arm grows, overlapping plates slide apart a little but still overlap, so there is no gap. Picking 'get bigger by themselves' is the very thing a crab's armour cannot do. Nothing hard and dead can grow on its own.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what worked, what did not, and what they would change.
flow.say: What worked? What did not? What would you change next time?
flow.kid: What worked? What did not? What would you change?
flow.parent: There is no single right design. Praise designs that solved one problem well, and ask what a real animal might do instead.

challenges.title: Crawl Without Legs
challenges.problem: An earthworm crawls with no legs and no wheels. Make a model 'worm' that moves itself 30 cm across a table, without you pushing the worm directly.
constraints: You may pull a string or blow, but you may not push the worm with your fingers.
The worm must be at least 10 cm long.
Use only paper, straws, string, tape, rubber bands, cloth and things from home.
general: Make an inchworm. Fold a strip of paper into a zigzag. Pull a thread through it to squash it, then let go so it springs out. Tape a little sandpaper or a rubber band under the back end, so it grips while the front slides.
Copy the worm's bristles. Stick short pieces of a toothbrush or stiff paper fringe underneath, all leaning backwards. They slide forwards but catch backwards, so each push moves the worm one way.
Make a sock worm. Put a string through a sock, with a knot at the front. Pull and relax the string. Bunch and stretch, bunch and stretch.
creative: Scrunch the paper cover of a drinking straw down into a tight wiggly worm. Put it on a plate and add one drop of water. It stretches and wriggles. The water fills the paper, like liquid filling a worm's body.
Robot makers build soft robots that move like worms and octopus arms. Some are pumped up with air, like your balloons in the Water Bones experiment.
Could your worm move along a tube or a hose, the way a worm moves through soil?

check.q: Why do backward-leaning bristles help a model worm move forward?
options: They slide forward easily but catch when pushed backward
check.why: Backward-leaning bristles slide easily one way and dig in the other way. So each squeeze moves the worm forward and not back. Real earthworms have tiny bristles on every segment that work the same way. Picking 'they look like legs' is close, but bristles do not walk. They only grip.

opts: A chain of small bones down the middle of the back
quiz.why: A backbone is a chain of small bones called vertebrae. Picking 'a shell' mixes it up with snails and crabs, whose hard parts are outside.
A snake has a long backbone with hundreds of vertebrae, even though it has no legs. Picking the earthworm usually means a long, legless shape fooled you.

quiz.p: Out of every 100 named kinds of animal, about how many have no backbone?
quiz.why: About 95 out of 100 kinds of animal are invertebrates. Picking 5 swaps the numbers: animals with a backbone are the small group.

quiz.p: Remember the Backbone Census? You counted the kinds of animal in one small patch, and sorted them into animals with a backbone and without one. Most families find many more kinds without a backbone. Why?
opts: Small animals can live in many tiny places, like under stones and on leaves
Small animals are not really animals
Only small animals live in gardens
quiz.why: Small invertebrates fit into many more tiny homes than big animals do. Picking 'not really animals' is a common habit of thinking. Ants and worms are animals too.
quiz.context: Remember the Backbone Census? You counted the kinds of animal in one small patch, and sorted them into animals with a backbone and without one.

quiz.p: How does an earthworm stay firm without bones?
opts: It is full of liquid squeezed tight by its muscles
It dries out in the sun
quiz.why: A worm has a water skeleton. Its muscles squeeze the liquid inside, like a full water balloon. Picking 'a shell inside' is a guess, but worms have no hard parts at all.

quiz.p: Which animal wears its skeleton on the outside, like armour?
quiz.why: A crab has an exoskeleton, a hard skeleton on the outside. Picking the jellyfish forgets that a jellyfish has no skeleton at all.

quiz.p: An animal has 6 legs and 3 body parts. What is it?
quiz.why: 6 legs and 3 body parts means an insect. Picking a spider is the most common mix-up. Spiders have 8 legs and 2 body parts.

quiz.p: Which of these is NOT an insect?
quiz.why: A spider is an arachnid, with 8 legs. Ants, mosquitoes and bees all have 6 legs.

quiz.p: Remember the Water Bones experiment? You filled long balloons with a little water, half full, and full and tight, and measured how much each drooped over a table edge. Why did the full, tight balloon droop the least?
opts: Water packed in tight pushes out on every side and holds the shape
quiz.why: Water cannot be squashed, so when it is packed in tight it holds the balloon firm. That is how a worm stays firm. Picking 'lightest' is wrong: the full balloon was the heaviest.
quiz.context: Remember the Water Bones experiment? You filled long balloons with a little water, half full, and full and tight, and measured how much each drooped over a table edge.

quiz.p: In a fair test of the paper tubes, what should you keep the same?

quiz.why: In a fair test you change only one thing, the shape, and keep everything else the same. Picking 'only the shape' gets it backwards: the shape is the one thing you change.
quiz.context: Remember the Armour Tubes experiment? You made a round tube, a square tube and a zigzag from paper, and added notebooks on top until each one crumpled.

quiz.p: A starfish is a closer cousin of yours than of a snail. What does this tell us about the word 'invertebrate'?
opts: It is not one family. It just means every animal that is not a vertebrate
quiz.why: 'Invertebrate' groups animals by something they lack. It holds many separate branches. Picking 'starfish have backbones' is not right: they have no bones, but they share our branch of the family tree.

quiz.p: Which of these is still an open question that scientists argue about?
opts: Whether insects like ants can feel pain
quiz.why: Leg counts, backbones and moulting are settled. Whether insects can feel pain is still argued. Picking the others mixes up open questions with things scientists have checked many times.

quiz.p: You find a snail after rain and want to look at it. What is the kind way?
opts: Keep it in a closed jar for a week
Hold it gently by its shell, watch it for a few minutes, put it back where you found it and wash your hands
Pull it out of its shell to see inside
Put salt on it to see what happens
quiz.why: Watch kindly, for a short time, and return the animal where you found it. Salt hurts snails badly, and a snail cannot leave its shell. Wash your hands, because snails can carry germs.

Honeybees and many other insects pollinate crops like mangoes, mustard, apples and cotton.
Silk comes from the cocoons of silkworm moths. India is one of the biggest silk makers in the world.
Lac, used in bangles, polish and sealing wax, is made by tiny lac insects on trees in Jharkhand and Chhattisgarh.
Engineers copy spider silk to try to make strong, light threads.
Soft robots are built to move like worms and octopus arms, to squeeze into pipes or rubble.
A glowing green material from a jellyfish is used by scientists all over the world to light up cells and watch them.
Doctors once used leeches, and still sometimes do, to help blood flow in sewn-on fingers and ears.
Pearls are grown in oysters, and shells were once used as money in parts of India and Africa.
Prawns, crabs and mussels are important food, and fishing them feeds millions of families along India's coasts.
Scientists watch the insects in streams to check whether river water is clean.
Coral reefs protect coasts from waves and are home to a huge number of fish.
