open_questions.q: How many kinds of animal without a backbone are there on Earth?
open_questions.why_open: Most of them have never been seen by scientists. Estimates go from a few million to many millions.

open_questions.q: Which group branched off the animal family tree first: sponges or comb jellies?
open_questions.why_open: Different studies of genes give different answers. Scientists are still arguing.

open_questions.q: Can insects, worms or jellyfish feel pain or anything at all?
open_questions.why_open: We can only watch what animals do from the outside. Nobody knows how to measure what an animal feels.

open_questions.q: Why are there no giant insects on land today?
open_questions.why_open: Oxygen in the air, heavy armour and hungry birds may all play a part. Nobody knows which matters most.

open_questions.q: How can a starfish, with no brain, decide which way to go?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists are studying how its arms share messages, but they do not fully understand it yet.

open_questions.q: How does a tardigrade survive drying out, freezing and even space?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have found special proteins that help, but they do not yet know the whole story.

open_questions.q: Why can some animals, like flatworms and starfish, regrow whole body parts, while we cannot?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists are finding some of the genes involved, but nobody knows the full answer.

maths.problem: In the Backbone Census, a family found 2 kinds of animal with a backbone and 11 kinds without. How many more kinds without a backbone did they find?
maths.explain: They found 11 kinds without a backbone and 2 kinds with one. 11 take away 2 is 9. So they found 9 more kinds of invertebrate. You can check: 2 + 9 = 11.
maths.context: Remember the Backbone Census? You counted the kinds of animal in one small patch, and sorted them into animals with a backbone and without one.

chart.title: Kinds of animal found in one patch in 10 minutes

maths.why_maths: Saying 'more' is a start. Working out 'how many more' tells us how big the difference really is.

maths.problem: In the Leg Count Key, you looked at 3 ants and 2 spiders. An ant has 6 legs and a spider has 8. How many legs are there altogether?
maths.explain: 3 ants have 3 groups of 6 legs. 6 + 6 + 6 = 18. 2 spiders have 2 groups of 8 legs. 8 + 8 = 16. 18 + 16 = 34 legs altogether.
maths.context: Remember the Leg Count Key? You counted legs to sort small animals: 6 legs for an insect, 8 for a spider.
maths.why_maths: Every animal of a group has the same number of legs. So we can count in equal groups instead of counting every leg one by one.

maths.problem: In the Water Bones experiment, the balloon with a little water drooped 8 cm. The full, tight balloon drooped 1 cm. How much less did the full balloon droop?
maths.explain: The little-water balloon drooped 8 cm. The full one drooped just 1 cm. 8 take away 1 is 7. So the full balloon drooped 7 cm less. It was much firmer.
maths.context: Remember the Water Bones experiment? You filled long balloons with a little water, half full, and full and tight, and measured how much each drooped over a table edge.

chart.title: How far each balloon drooped over the table edge

maths.why_maths: Measuring in centimetres lets us say exactly how much firmer a full balloon is, instead of just saying 'firmer'.

maths.problem: In the Many Small Suckers experiment, one sucker held 3 cups of rice. If every sucker held the same, how many cups should 4 suckers hold?
maths.explain: 4 suckers each holding 3 cups is 4 groups of 3. 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 12. So 4 suckers should hold 12 cups. In the made-up results they held 11, a little less, because real suckers do not share the load perfectly.
maths.context: Remember the Many Small Suckers experiment? You hung a bag from rubber suckers on a tile and added cups of rice until they popped off.

chart.title: Cups of rice held before the suckers popped off

maths.why_maths: Multiplying tells us what to expect if every grip adds up perfectly. Comparing that with what really happened shows us something new.

maths.problem: The Bottle Wormery started on a Monday and lasts 14 days. You look on day 1, day 3, day 7, day 10 and day 14. How many days are there between the day 7 look and the day 14 look?
maths.explain: Day 14 take away day 7 is 7. So there are 7 days between the two looks. That is one whole week, so the last look is on a Monday too.
maths.context: Remember the Bottle Wormery? You made stripes of soil and sand in a bottle, added earthworms and looked at it over 14 days.
maths.why_maths: Slow changes need careful timing. Counting the days between looks helps us plan, and helps us say how fast the worms worked.

roots.context: We have been learning about animals without backbones: worms, snails, crabs, spiders, insects, starfish and jellyfish. Now we ask what they tell us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: 'Animals without backbones' is not a kind of animal. It is nearly every animal, named by the one thing it lacks compared to us.
deep_truth.habit: We sort the world into 'us' and 'the rest', with ourselves at the centre. The word 'invertebrate' names 95 out of 100 kinds of animal by what they are not. Look closer and 'the rest' is many families, and some of them, like the starfish, are our own close cousins.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Backbone Census, most of the animals you found had no backbone. And on the family tree, a starfish sits on our branch, closer to you than to a snail.

three.who_am_i: You are one of the rare animals with a backbone. Your nearest boneless cousin lives in the sea and has five arms.
three.what_is_life: Life holds itself up in many ways. Bones inside, armour outside, a shell, or just water held tight.
three.what_is_this_world: Most of the animals on Earth are small, boneless and busy, under your feet and in the sea.

roots.thread: Long ago, all animals came from one small, soft animal in the sea. From that one came the many: worms, snails, spiders, ants, starfish, fish and you. Some found water to hold them up, some built shells, some wore armour, and one branch grew bones inside. DeepKids believes this is the One showing up as the many, each trying a different way to stand up in the world. The worm, the crab and you are not separate kinds of life. You are different answers to the same question.

teachings.source: Acaranga Sutra, Book 1, Lecture 2, Lesson 3 (a Jain scripture, in Hermann Jacobi's translation)
teachings.teaching: All beings are fond of life. They like pleasure and dislike pain. To all, life is dear. This is why Jain monks walk softly and sweep the ground ahead of them, so as not to step on tiny creatures.
teachings.link: The smallest animals, the ants and worms and woodlice, are most of the animals there are. Caring for life means caring mostly for them.

teachings.link: We look at a butterfly from outside, as a different kind of animal. Zhuangzi asks whether the line between 'me' and 'that small creature' is as fixed as it seems.

teachings.teaching: Picture a huge net with a shining jewel at every knot. Each jewel reflects every other jewel.
teachings.link: A dewy spider web in the morning looks just like this. Every animal in the garden, from the worm to the bird, holds up every other.

science.text: All animals share one ancestor. Starfish, sea urchins and vertebrates are on one big branch of the family tree, so a starfish is a closer cousin of ours than a snail is.
About 95 out of every 100 named kinds of animal have no backbone, and millions more may be waiting to be found.

other_view.who: Many biologists, and the old Charvaka school in India
other_view.view: Being related is a fact about history, like a family tree. It does not mean we are one being. A starfish is a starfish and you are you. Nothing more is needed to explain it. That is an honest view, and many careful people hold it.

practice.title: Backbone, then jellyfish
practice.say: Sit up tall. Put one hand on the back of your neck and slowly walk your fingers down your back, bump by bump. Each bump is a small bone holding you up. Now let your whole body go soft, like a jellyfish floating in the sea. Let your arms hang like tentacles. Breathe in slowly, and out slowly, three times. Feel what is holding you now: the chair, the floor, the air. Now sit up tall again. Which felt more like you?
